CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That the first report of the Standing Committee on National
Defence and Veterans Affairs, presented to the House on Tliesday,
October 2, be concurred in.
Routine Proceedings
He said: Madam Speaker, I am proud to be able to rise today and speak in support of my motion for concurrence in the first report of the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs.
On October 2, the hon. member for Crowfoot, the very capable chair of the committee, tabled the report in this House. In preparing to draft the report, the committee spent many hours hearing testimony from a broad range of witnesses.
I am very pleased to be able to report that members of the committee from all parties gave a sympathetic hearing to the witnesses representing former merchant mariners. When the time came to prepare our report and its recommendations there was a tremendous degree of all-party consensus and, Madam Speaker, no one knows better than you how rare and precious is a non-partisan moment among members of Parliament.
I would like in my remarks to address the realities that members of the committee came face to face with while studying the problems of our former merchant seamen. First I want to take a moment to remind the House of the committee's recommendations. The committee recommended that Canadian merchant mariners with one or more high seas, ocean-going assignments during wartime be fully recognized as veterans, and that veterans benefits be extended to them.
The committee also recommended that a book of remembrance, dedicated solely to merchant mariners who died in Canada's wars, be placed in the Peace Tower.
Finally, the committee recommended that the Department of Veterans Affairs encourage the construction of a suitable monument to honour the memory of Canada's war-time merchant mariners.
The committee suggested as well that Halifax would be a suitable site for such a monument.
As I have already said, the committee was unanimous in adopting these recommendations. We all agreed that the case of the merchant mariners was one that should have been addressed a long while ago, that it was crucial that Parliament act quickly because it is almost too late.

Routine Proceedings
With such non-partisan agreement, I feel more than comfortable in moving concurrence in the committee's report.
Let me go back in history to the end of the Second World War. Following World War II, the Government of Canada extended a total of 18 benefits to veterans of our Armed Forces. Of those 18, only four were granted unconditionally to merchant seamen. A further seven benefits were extended to them only under certain conditions.
For example, under the Veterans Land Act, the merchant mariner did obtain benefits under the Veterans Land Act if he was disabled. How are you going to farm if you are disabled? Over 12,000 merchant seamen served Canada in World War II. Only about 3,500 are still living, and the Department of Veterans Affairs says that in 1989-90, 221 merchant seamen recipients of the civilian war allowance died, more than one every two days.
There were 1,259 of them who died in combat, the highest casualty rate in the Second World War of any of our Armed Forces. Canadian seamen served with distinction on all oceans of the world during World War II; 1,259 of them died and nearly 200 were imprisoned.
The loss of merchant seamen lives during the battle of the Atlantic was the highest proportionately of any of the allied forces during that last great conflict.
Canadian seamen who served in dangerous waters during the last great war seek today what they have sought from the end of that war, equal recognition, entitlements and the benefits now received by their fellow veterans.
Last year for the first time, the Royal Canadian Legion agreed that World War II merchant seamen should be given veteran status. It is high time we extended veterans' benefits to Canadian merchant mariners who made at least one high seas trip during World War II.
I want to remind the House that 45 years have gone by. This question has been studied for nearly half a century.
During the war most categories of merchant seamen were paid much less than their counterparts in the Royal Canadian Navy, while the risks they faced were just as great if not greater. Members of our merchant navy could not leave the service. They were bound by military discipline and orders for the duration of the war.
Canada has still failed to repay its debt to some veterans of war against Fascism. It is shameful that for 45 years government after government of both the major parties have refused to recognize adequately the contribution these courageous Canadians made during those terrible years.
I find it therefore especially gratifying to see members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, members of Parliament from all three parties, coming together with such unanimity on the need to act now.
I should add that a similar committee in the other place also held hearings and heard witnesses. It too was unanimous that merchant mariners should be granted recognition as full veterans. After the war, merchant seamen were not provided with the same benefits given other Canadians. This is puzzling since merchant seamen had been awarded the same medals given to Royal Canadian Navy veterans. Both the United States and the United Kingdom recognized their merchant seamen as veterans. Since January 1988 U.S. merchant seamen are eligible for full benefits from their veterans administration. Of course, the Royal Canadian Legion has passed a resolution calling for the Parliament of Canada to recognize our merchant seamen as war veterans.
On this issue the ball is in government's and Parliament's court. During the battle of the Atlantic, Canada's merchant navy suffered the highest casualty rate of any allied force. On October 2, the standing committee on national defence made that very obvious.
The one recommendation made by the committee was that merchant mariners be granted war veterans status and be eligible for all war veterans benefits. The hon. minister, of course, has 150 days in which to respond to the report in question. As I have said, this is an issue that has been studied to death. I respectfully suggest that the minister does not need the full 150 days to respond to the committee's report.
I am informed that the minister has engaged a retired general to determine who should be given veteran status and what the cost would be of implementing the committee's recommendations. I want to caution the minister strongly that it would be foolish and destructive to again fail to consult with the merchant mariners themselves on this issue. At some point I hope the minister will present his positive recommendations regarding merchant mari-

ners to cabinet for approval of the action required to implement the committee's recommendations.
Of course, I do not quarrel with the government's responsibility to examine the fiscal implications of any public policy initiatives, however in considering the costs of the committee's recommendations, the government must not lose sight of the ethical obligation Canadians have to our World War II merchant mariners, who have never received the recognition and reward they earned during their wartime service.
There can be no price tag on doing the right thing. We, as a people, must not let the cost of these benefits cause us to deny them to those who have earned them.
Let us consider for a moment the budget practices of the Department of Veterans Affairs over the years. According to the public accounts of Canada, the department has allowed to lapse, in other words budgetary funds they did not spend, a total of $380.8 million of its appropriated funds since the fiscal year 1982-83. In other words, the department has underspent its budget by an average of $47.8 million over the last eight fiscal years. Again, these figures from public accounts show that under the Liberal government of the day, they underspent its veterans affairs budget by $22.9 million, by $56.1 million in 1983-84, by $70 million in 1984-85. Then the Conservatives gained power and they underspent the veterans affairs budget by $45.5 million in 1985-86, $33.6 million in 1986-87, $56.6 million in 1987-88, $56 million 1988-89, and $40.1 million 1989-90.
The money was always there, much more than enough to award our merchant mariners full veteran's status and full veterans' benefits retroactively.
The Royal Canadian Legion says it will cost about $10 million a year to implement the committee's recommendation. The Department of Veterans Affairs has said it will take $20 million. In either case the department has plenty of room in its budget right now to do justice by our merchant mariners.
As I have said so many times over the years, our merchant mariners were mistreated and ignored by a
Routine Proceedings
succession of Canadian governments and by the Canadian people and by the Canadian Parliament. The figures I have just cited show that in fact the money was always available and is available today to extend full benefits.
The House of Commons veterans affairs committee was unanimous in its support of our merchant mariners and has tabled an excellent report which offers very positive recommendations. I am only sorry that the report is silent on the fate of merchant seamen and the merchant fleet after World War II and into the fifties.
After the war came the final insult for Canadian merchant seamen. Those who survived the war and stayed in the fleet found their jobs sold out from under them and U.S. gangsters imported to destroy their union. The destruction of the merchant fleet and the importation of Hal Banks and his methods meant that many merchant seamen were deprived of their livelihood after gallantly serving their country at great personal risk.
This would have been a strong argument in favour of extending to merchant navy veterans the same vocational training benefits that were given to other veterans. I was one who got the benefits of vocational training after my discharge. It is too late now to do that for the merchant mariners.
There remains the question of retroactivity for some other benefits. Why not, for example, extend to merchant seamen retroactive disability benefits to eligible veterans? There are other benefits that merchant seamen were denied that could and should be at least partially restored. The clothing allowance that other veterans receive could be extended as well as some elements of the veterans' business and personal loan benefits.
Last week while speaking to my private member's bill on this subject I told the House last spring Gordon Olmstead came to Parliament looking for something denied him for almost half a century, recognition. The Second World War veteran and prisoner of war should have been entitled to the benefits offered to other veterans by a grateful nation. But Gordon Olmstead served with Canada's merchant marines and the federal government still refuses to acknowledge the contribu-

November 7, 1991
Routine Proceedings
tions and sacrifices made by those who served in that fleet.
This spring Mr. Olmstead and other merchant marine veterans appeared as witnesses before the House of Commons standing committee. Their goal was to obtain legal recognition of their status as war veterans. During their testimony we heard again and again the statistics that I have already cited. To suggest for one moment that they were civilians not eligible for benefits from the armed forces is totally negated by the fact that they were under military command, control, and orders. In fact the Royal Canadian Navy on many ships provided a gun crew of three, four, five or six men. Many merchant seamen were trained on how to handle four-inch guns, 50-calibre machine guns, Bofors or pom-pom guns. They carried on the military part of defending their ships in their convoys. If that does not make them part of the armed forces, I do not know what would.
Our wartime minister called them the fourth arm of our armed forces. There are only about 3,500 of them left and some surviving spouses and maybe some surviving children. It is no wonder that Canada's Minister of Transport called them the fourth arm.
Sadly this sentiment was conveniently set aside when the war ended in 1945. When it was time to honour and reward our merchant seamen their service was ignored.
This is the least our nation, our Parliament and our government can do in order to show its gratitude and rectify a terribly sad wrong. Merchant seamen only received three or four of the 18 benefits without condition and their dead were not given the honours they had purchased at so dear a price.
I understand the appointing of a retired general to look into this matter and cost it. I am informed that merchant seamen have already been told that they are not going to get veteran status. Well I hope that is not true. It better not be true.
It is alleged by this general that there is too much opposition to it. Nobody can tell us where the opposition comes from. I do not know of a single Canadian opposed to this measure. I call on members from all parties in a non-partisan manner to call upon and require this government to do what the committee recommends and what the other place has recommended. It is a long overdue reward to our merchant seamen. We can do no less.
I hope we can get the sentiment of the House with a vote on my motion.

It is interesting to just comment on the problem of the failure of consecutive governments to fully recognize the contribution of the mariners who served during wartime in Canada's merchant service.
It is no less service than the fighting of Fascism during the Second World War by the merchant marines. I would like to add that in the 12 years I have been in the House

of Commons, it is one of the most disappointing things that I can recall. I know many of the other members in this party and the others feel the same way, that recognition has been made with the benefits accredited to other veterans of that conflict. We must grant appropriate recognition to the service that was given, the loss of life, the injuries, the loss to their families and to themselves of five years of their life in service to their country, in service to democracy and the world.
The contribution made there is a forceful and powerful one. Failure of this House to provide recognition is one of the truly sad situations that neither the Liberal government nor this government has been able to see its way clear to provide that diminishing number of Canadians with the recognition that they so truly earned by complete sacrifice during that period of time. The sacrifice was as great as any of the other organized armed forces of this country. I wonder if the hon. member might be able to comment on it.
The other thing is the extent. It is interesting how politics tend to interfere with some of these things. I really wonder what the reason for not doing it is.
I know my colleague for years has fought also for another group of veterans that has been completely denied any recognition by this House, and that is of course the veterans of the Spanish civil war. To my knowledge there is only one legislature in this country, in British Columbia, that officially recognized the contribution of 1,200 Canadians who went to Spain just before the outbreak of the Second World War to fight Fascism. Had that conflict been resolved by support of the governments of the day, we may not have seen the Second World War.
I would add my voice to urge that this government see its way clear to providing veterans benefits and medals of recognition to Canada's wartime merchant service and that that occur as soon as possible.

Madam Speaker, I am glad I was in the House when this motion came forward today. I want to commend the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden for bringing this issue to the floor of the House.
Coming from Nova Scotia, more particularly representing a riding that is on the shores of Halifax harbour, I certainly understand the value of those individuals who served in Canada's merchant marine.
The one thing I have a great deal of difficulty with as a member of Parliament, because all the time we get into the cut and thrust of debate and partisanship, is that I do not know if there is anybody in this House who could possibly have any justification for disagreeing with the motion that has been put forward by my colleague from Regina-Lumsden.
Surely to goodness there are times where the issues are black and white and right and wrong. In my view this is clearly one of those issues that is that definitive. The individuals who served in Canada's merchant marine were a critical part of Canada's war effort. They worked on the fringe of it; they were in the middle of it. When those convoys assembled in Bedford Basin in Halifax harbour and went overseas they were literally sitting ducks. They knew that the job at hand was one that in many cases, and history will prove in nearly all cases, put them at greater risk than the men in uniform who were going over on Canada's supply ships or destroyers.
I was reading some articles on these merchant mariners. An article I read this morning talked about the supreme sacrifice that they made in order to ensure that the supply lines to Britain, to Europe and up to the Soviet Union were maintained and that food was getting through so that people did not starve to death behind the blockades of the Germans.
One in ten of those merchant mariners lost his life. That is 10 per cent. It is the highest loss of life of any branch of the Canadian Armed Forces in any conflict we have ever been involved with. What are they looking for? Let us be fair here. They are not looking for the moon. They want recognition of their service. They want to be treated as veterans out of uniform.
I just read another little piece here as the member for Regina-Lumsden was speaking. It said: "When the periscope would break the water because the Nazi submarines used to travel in packs of 10 or 12, the convoys would then speed up to try to get away from them because they were pretty deadly. When the convoys would speed away it was the vessels of the merchant marine which were usually slower that were left behind, literally sitting ducks." They were literally sitting ducks. One in ten of the men who served in Canada's merchant marine lost his life. It was one in ten. That is pretty startling.
What are they looking for today after years and years? They simply want some recognition. They want to be recognized as veterans. We have had the report of the standing committee on veterans affairs. It is conclusive and unanimous.
We have had in the other place a motion that was put forward by Senator Marshall which was ruled out of order because it was seen to be a money bill. It seems everybody in both places-forget the technicalities and niceties that we often immerse ourselves in because we do not want to make decisions-is clear that this is a wrong that we can right very easily.
We are not going to bust the bank. It is not going to cost the government billions of dollars. I am not trying to get partisan here, because every government wastes money, but I see that money was put into some ACOA projects in Nova Scotia that were absolutely ridiculous. You lost $14 million on the NFC diesel plant and you lost $11 million on this one and $10 million frittered away on that one. You see money found for particle accelerators in British Columbia, however useful that may be I do not know. You see money going for a comedy festival in Montreal.
I am not saying that they are not priorities of the government, but surely to goodness if I were an individual who served in the merchant marine and put my life on the line because I believed in the cause of the allied forces, but more particularly because I wanted to serve my country, I think I would find it pretty difficult to sit down at age 70 or 72 and try to figure out why I still love this country in that the country will not even give me the very minimum of recognizing me as a veteran and giving me full veterans' benefits including extended care.
November 7, 1991

The government has gone some distance. It has provided some benefits. Those benefits are not insignificant. Some of them are fairly major. I cannot for the life of me figure out why we just do not go that extra mile, do the right thing and recognize the service of Canada's merchant mariners.
They become less and less every year. My father is a veteran. He served with the Cape Breton Highlanders. Every year they have a reunion and every year my father is depressed after the reunion. Do you know why he is depressed? It is because every year in that one small unit there are five or six less than were there the previous year because they are dying. It is the age they are at.
We are not looking at 10,000 individuals. I think somebody has mentioned that the numbers are closer to 3,500. That is it. If the government wants to study this forever-the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden knows this-and if this thing keeps going, it will not have to make a decision because there will not be any of them left. They will be gone.
Surely to goodness, all members of this House can for once do the right thing and put a little bit of respect back in the jobs that we do here. This is something that we can all do. I would urge the minister not to study this thing any more. Let us rise above all that. It is not going to cost a lot of money. Governments have always found money for the right thing when it was obvious that the right thing was the way to go.
This is the right thing. I support the motion of the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden. I think all members of this House would support of motion of the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden. For once let us do something right. Let us pay back those people who risked their lives and whose colleagues on those vessels supplying food to Europe and to the Soviet Union gave the supreme sacrifice.
I hope that this is one of those rare occasions when this House rises above the partisanship and the nonsense that we engage in many times, does the right thing and supports this motion.

Madam Speaker, I would like to welcome my colleague from New Brunswick into the debate and I appreciate his comments.
There is no question at all that the merchant mariners are entitled to some benefits. They receive a civilian war allowance equal in value to the war veterans allowance, however they are not eligible for long-term care. It is not a matter of comparison, it is a little different here. We were not under siege in Canada and these individuals were not conscripted to join the war effort. The people we are talking about in Canada's merchant marine could have stayed home in Halifax or in Saint John, New Brunswick or in other places and they could have plied the Canadian waters if that was what they wished to do. They would not have had to worry about putting their lives on the line in the war effort. They made a very conscious decision to support Canada's war effort.
From what I have read and from what I have been told by some of the merchant mariners who have approached my office to try to ascertain how much support would be in this House for the type of motion that the member for Regina-Lumsden brought, they are not looking for a lot, they are looking for very little. I have heard that some veterans are concerned and are saying we have to address all of the outstanding concerns they have before we go and give to somebody else.
This is not one of those cases in which if you give and if you do what is right with the merchant mariners, that of necessity, it is going to take away from what should be the government's commitment to those other individuals who served in uniform, those other veterans.

As I said earlier, we are not dealing with an expanding group. Because of the advances of time, and age takes its toll, we are dealing with a diminishing group of individuals here.
As far as what Great Britain does, I do not think we should look over there and say that if it gives less benefits therefore that is what we should do. I think there is a recognition in this country that the efforts that Canada put forward with the allied forces in the Second World War were fairly unique. I think that the contribution of the merchant mariners was very unique and they deserve nothing less than full recognition and full benefits as has been proposed.

At this time when the credibility of politicians is at its lowest, my colleague from Regina-Lumsden has been involved in this issue for years and years. I think we could address a long-standing grievance of the merchant marine seamen as well as improve the credibility of this House and politicians generally if we did the right thing and acknowledged the kind of grievance that a line of governments have perpetrated on those people.
As someone who was born after the war, I think we forget the kind of horrors that these people experienced, the kind of courage they had to have to do the work they did. As I go each year as the member for my riding to lay a wreath at the veterans' cenotaph in my riding, I think of not just the people in uniform but all the people who contributed to the war effort to ensure the kind of democracy that we enjoy in Canada.
I hope this motion from my colleague from Regina- Lumsden finally brings this to a happy conclusion and gives those merchant seamen the recognition and the remuneration they so richly deserve.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure to take part in this debate that has flowed from a very interesting process. The hon. member for Regina-Lumsden has set out that he thought it was a good example of co-operative work on a parliamentary committee and I believe that it is.
It is an issue that has been around for a long time, nearly 50 years now. Clearly it is there and it is not going to go away. It is high time that, through the committee
Routine Proceedings
system which I think has come from reform of this Parliament, that pressure be brought to bear to raise the issue to the surface and have it dealt with and set aside in a final form.
I suppose there is no other single reason for asking that our recommendations be concurred in than the simple one of it being the right thing to do. Anyone who takes a look at the merchant mariners and the service they have committed on behalf of Canada and Canadians will note the level of risk they undertook, the per cent of loss of life and the fact, as was mentioned earlier, that they were assigned by Order in Council to conduct their duties.
An assignment lasted for a period of two years. If they left ship, they were under military discipline and could not leave until their duty was completed and they accepted higher risks. All of these things would clearly lead one to the conclusion that these honourable men and women served their country in wartime, served it well and are due the recognition in a formal way that the country ought to bestow to them.
We know, because it has been mentioned, that some 70 ships of the Canadian merchant marine were lost. In addition to that, one member mentioned that 10 per cent of the lives of the merchant marines were lost in service. The comparative number is also important. It compares with about 4 per cent in all forces, or to compare it with the Royal Canadian Navy at the time, a 40 per cent higher loss of life took place in the merchant navy.
Therefore, when we couple all of that with the fact that one merchant navy ship could carry enough goods and supplies to take care of the needs of 250,000 fighting men and women in the European theatre, we recognize that the defence of freedom could not have taken place without the umbilical cord of the merchant navy. It could not have taken place without the merchant navy. All of our fighting men and women would have been lost in the battle of war without a supply of food, ammunition, metals and materials brought to them by those persons who were so ordered by the Government of Canada some 50 years ago and who did so under military assignment and direction. They went with poorly armed ships often with either no escort or very thin lines of escort service into the battle of the Atlantic.

Routine Proceedings
Once the Germans had captured a significant part of Europe, particularly the lowlands of Europe, then they made their targets the merchant ships of North America. The merchant ships became the German targets.
Clearly they were an essential part of the war effort. While I will have to use a sharp scalpel, it is important, I believe, to set aside what I think is perhaps a significant misconception being set out in the debate.
I believe to this point that for those persons in our country who may be listening to us they could not help but come to the conclusion that Canada has set aside all regard for the merchant mariner. I believe this report would ask the government to close the circle because in many ways a merchant mariner today receives many of the benefits that are received by veterans of Canada. They recognize that, veterans' groups recognize that. There is a gap that remains and that is what we are asking to be reviewed for a period of time and that at the conclusion of that time, that the government respond in a positive way.
For those who know, because of the studies we have conducted and the witnesses we have heard, the enormity of assistance that has been given to our country in its efforts to defend freedom by our merchant marines, would also come to the very strong conclusion that it would only be appropriate that in the Peace Tower of this building, though probably and appropriately in a separate book, there would be a book of remembrance for those who lost their lives through their efforts as merchant marines in the defence of Canada.
I cannot believe that there will be any debate that would argue otherwise.
We live in a country that has a history so rich, descriptive, amazing, and so wonderful. However, Canadians can be accused of nothing other than being overly bashful, too inward looking, and almost zealously looking to the United States as the nation with the national symbols, afraid to build our own.
In recognizing the role that Canada played in the war years and the importance of the merchant mariners in that effort, I think nothing could be more appropriate than placing where the activity was strongest, which perhaps would be the east coast since most of them left from the port of Halifax, a recognition, be it a small
museum or a cannon or something that signals our pride and our historical indebtedness to persons who manned the 70 ships that went to the bottom of oceans, to those who were injured or maimed and for those who were not but who came home to lesser conditions as veterans who so valiantly and diligently served their country on behalf of the defence of freedom.
I would concur with those who have said that it is interesting. I think it is more than interesting. I think it is appropriate that this debate is taking place close to Remembrance Day because in all of those words we have expressed over so many years, "Lest we Forget," and "We shall not forget," there has been a group forgotten too frequently. For the mariners who served in very poor working conditions, with very poor salaries, with extraordinary risk, it is only appropriate that the most thorough of examinations of the recommendations of the committee be undertaken.
It is my understanding that the department is in the process at the moment of reviewing the recommendations. I remain optimistic that they will respond and will do so positively.
Having said that, I want to remind the hon. members and particularly the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden that what his motion does is to ask for concurrence. In doing so he must ask for concurrence of the report, not for a part of the report or a section of the report but for the report. It is a part of the report to which the department has 150 days to respond.
Now we all know that we have had representatives from the Canadian Army, Navy and various other organizations before our committee and we have examined them. The department I understand is also into that process at this time. We have waited 50 years and I think that has been a sad blight on Canadian history. It is sometimes inappropriate to say if we have waited 50 years then let us just wait a short while longer. But I do believe this is a course for which we can see the end. I believe that recommendations are coming and are coming soon.
As to the question of giving veteran status to merchant mariners, one has to ask the question: Why would this be such an objection to some if the Royal Canadian Legion, members of other direct forces such as Army, Navy and Air Force, and other veterans groups will accept among their ranks merchant mariners as veterans. If they among themselves accept each other as colleagues and

partners who served for a national effort during wartime, then it is questionable as to the appropriateness for someone else, somewhere else to draw a line and to try and define a difference.
I do not know if we separate on this issue or not with the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden when he says that we must go forward and do the right thing regardless of money. I like that kind of thinking but not being a New Democrat I cannot follow through with it. I know it is always appropriate to do the right thing, but doing the ethical thing sometimes does require answering to the question of affordability because it has its own ethics to it. The money does not just get manufactured and come from some tube from nowhere to us. Affordability has to be, I believe, part of the consideration. I am not sure but I think maybe the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden would agree with that.
He will note that the recommendations were for an assignment, which is a specific word and has a connotation to it, for a trip in wartime and on the high seas. High sea does include the gulf on the west coast and the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Those are both high sea assignments. I believe that it does separate some of the crossings of a cove by a fishing boat that might have been on one occasion duty bound in the war effort. It might have carried a gun and transplanted it somewhere else. There may have been a risk at the time, but if we were to enter into that kind of consideration, I believe in affordability very much. I see the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden nodding in agreement. I did not know if that was a difference that we had or not but I believe from his non-verbal response that it is not a difference and I am pleased that is the case.
Let me basically conclude with this. I see a concurrence in this as a concurrence for the full report including the 150 days. I think there should be no debate at all about a monument or a book of remembrance. I think we are duty bound to recognize the enormity of the commitment that the merchant mariners made in defending freedom and putting down the aggression that was taking place in a rapid way through Europe during
Routine Proceedings
the periods of two of our world wars, but most significantly, the second one.
They did so with tremendous human cost. At the conclusion of the war they did not have the same benefits that were given to other veterans. That gap has been closed significantly as time has gone on and I would like to erase any connotations that might have been left, that there is a complete separation between veterans and merchant mariners because that is not factual.
What this report basically asks is for a recognition of status and that the gap be closed. I am sure that all members of the House join in that noble objective and that we can get on with one more task of righting a historical wrong. It is too bad it had to come so late in our history.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I hope the hon. member can listen to my speech.
As I was saying before the hon. member for Calgaiy Northeast interrupted, the report of the committee on national defence and veterans affairs contains a statement by the Hon. J.E. Michaud, Minister of Transport at the time, who said: "Merchant seamen virtually form the fourth arm of the fighting services, and despite their reticence to blazen abroad their heroic exploits, we feel that in fairness to them and to their next of kin the Canadian public should be told of their work."
At the end of World War II, Canadian soldiers were welcomed back to this country with the well know veterans charter. Not so our merchant seamen. Why? There are several explanations. First of all, in 1945, the government at the time was faced with the enormous task of taking care of over one million soldiers. New programs had to be implemented. Veterans' hospitals across the country were packed. It was a very busy time, during which the Canadian government faced unprecedented challenges.
Were the concerns of merchant seamen overlooked as a result? If they were, there was a lot to overlook, because 12,000 men served in the Canadian merchant navy and more than 1,100 were killed. Or perhaps it was assumed that since the crews of ships belonging to private shipping companies were civilians, not veterans, they were not entitled to veterans benefits. I imagine the authorities thought they did not have to take care of merchant seaman. After all, they had jobs waiting for them in the flourishing Canadian merchant fleet. The future looked good, but as we know now, Madam Speaker, disillusionment soon set in.
I don't know why the veterans charter did not apply to merchant seamen, but I know there was a very obvious problem that should have been resolved long before
1991.
Canada was not the only country whose treatment of merchant seamen differed from the way it treated veterans of its three forces. We know that Australia and the United States have recognized the rights of merchant seamen to certain benefits, but this is quite recent. And it was not the case for more than 40 years.
Perhaps it took all this time to destroy certain myths. It may be that during the war, members of the Armed Forces were envious of those who served in the merchant navy. They probably thought life in the merchant navy was easier. After all, weren't merchant seamen better paid? They did not have to bow to military discipline. They had a choice. In other words, it was assumed merchant seamen had more freedom than people in uniform who had to conform to the rules of the Royal Navy.

Routine Proceedings
We seem to forget that on many of these merchant ships served gunners who, while being recognized as service personnel, nevertheless obeyed the ship's captain on board. These gunners were recognized, but the civilian seamen were not.
The evidence heard by the House committee on national defence and veterans affairs as well as the sub-committee on veterans affairs indicate that we had misconceptions about life in the merchant navy. Discipline was rigourous and danger present. It took 46 years for the facts to be established. Why, do you figure, Mr. Gordon Olmstead from the Canadian Merchant Navy Prisoners of War Association told the committee: "Lack of recognition across Canada is apparent too, unfortunately. On such occasions as annual veterans' parades, Remembrance Day services, battle of the Atlantic services, there is total omission of the merchant navy's vital role."
Madam Speaker, I suggest this is sad and regrettable. It could be a reflection of attitudes that have lingered since the end of World War II. I think that men like Mr. Olmstead-merchant seamen have a real champion in him-deserve a place in the sun as well as in any parade.
I know that they were well represented last year at the Remembrance Day services in Ottawa, and I am sure they will be this year again. But this is obviously a most difficult issue for many other deserving people and I know that the minister will take that into account.
We have turned a deaf ear to the queries of merchant seamen for too long. I am pleased that this government has a different attitude. It has always been prepared to hear them out. The minister has been inundated with suggestions these past few months, namely from the Senate sub-committee on veterans affairs. At the invitation of the minister, veterans' organizations have set up a special committee to examine this persistent problem and the House standing committee has tabled its report. Merchant seamen organizations made presentations.
I think that the standing committee also tabled a veiy thorough report that contains solid arguments. The minister will probably take some time to go through these documents properly. I also suppose that veterans affairs will have to evaluate the cost of these recommendations in relation to other priorities, and that is normal. For example, the merchant seamen ask that the eligibility criteria for the Veterans Independence Program be broadened. They are not the only ones; applications under this program are skyrocketing.
In 1981, the government gave the program a budget of $1 million. This year, we will spend $137 million for
88,000	beneficiaries in the program. Unfortunately, it is not available to all veterans, but many of them would also like to benefit from it.
As for increased spending, Madam Speaker, veterans affairs has developed an ambitious plan to increase the number of hospital beds for veterans in the future. We want a sufficient reserve of beds within five to ten years. We know what hospitals cost the provinces; we must not forget about those costs.
We therefore understand why veterans affairs is trying to obtain significant funding to meet vetarans' future needs, which I must say should include those of merchant seamen who receive disability benefits. British Columbia and New Brunswick have already signed joint agreements and other provinces across Canada are preparing to do the same thing.
I think that we must realize the broad range of benefits and programs available to veterans and their families and that these must constantly be adjusted.
Given everything I just said, which is good news for veterans, and I think my colleague will admit it, I still deplore the lack of information Canadians have about the sacrifice these people had to make to give you and me and all Canadians the standard of living we enjoy today.
I often wonder why the government-owned television and radio do not interview these merchant seamen in the week following November 11 or the weekend before. Why do we not see them on television? Why are we not given information about them?

Perhaps our children should know the price that had to be paid for us to have the privilege of living in this country, Canada, and enjoying this standard of living.
I hope that some people in this country can produce radio and television programs so that this weekend and next week we can see films, documentaries and interviews with the men and women who served our country in those wars and can tell us what they suffered so that we will understand what price they had to pay to give us this kind of life. I hope that I have been heard.
I hope that my colleagues in this House will also do all they can when they meet our reporter friends around here to bend their ear and tell them that maybe this weekend and next week, they could do something, Madam Speaker, so that Canadians really understand the importance of the report that we tabled in this House.
In my opinion, the three recommendations-which is not a whole lot-are extremely important. The first one says that the Canadian merchant seamen who went to sea at least once in wartime be considered full fledged veterans and be allowed to enjoy all the benefits granted to veterans. Of course there is a price for that. But we found a way to correct the mistakes made against Canadians of Asian origin and Italian origin. Can we not do the same for Canadian citizens? I hope that all members of the House will apply the necessary pressure, as I will.
Of course, I cannot commit myself today to spending money before I know how much. Are we talking about $500 million, $20 million or $100 million? I believe my colleague will agree with us on that issue. We have to know what kind of money we are talking about. But, Madam Speaker, we must make every effort to give those seamen their due.
The second recommendation says that a remembrance book with the names of those merchant seamen who died during the wars in which Canada participated should be prepared and put in the Peace Tower. That is
obvious. It is not expensive and it should have been done years ago. I do not understand why it has not already been done.
Third, the Department of Veterans Affairs should promote the erection of a suitable monument to honour those who were in the Canadian merchant navy in wartime. The committee is of the opinion that this monument could be erected in the Halifax region. In fact, the suggestion to build the monument in the Halifax region was made by the merchant seamen, because most convoys that sailed to Europe or even Murmansk left from the Atlantic region, sometimes from the Gaspe peninsula, but usually from Halifax.
How much does a monument cost? What does it represent per Canadian? A quarter of a cent? How come this has not already been done? I am 49 years old and I have the privilege of living in a fantastic country. I always believed, until I started looking into this issue with my colleagues, that this had been done.
I can tell you that I am not particularly proud, as a younger Canadian, that the contribution and the sacrifices made by those people have not yet been recognized. After all, one merchant seaman in ten died. One in ten! Do you have any idea of how a merchant seaman felt when he was on a ship that was transporting ammunition and had to avoid a pack of six or seven U-boats? How do you think that seaman felt? He could not get off, because if he tried to escape, the police would go after him and take him to court, just like any other sailor serving in the Canadian navy. That seaman was subject to the same laws. He did not have a choice.
And what about those who worked on oil tankers? Once I saw a film that showed what it was like when an oil tanker was torpedoed. There were no survivors. There was literally a sea of fire. And I do not even talk about the ones who tried to save their comrades. I understand that my time is up, Madam Speaker, but I think the time has come, in 1991, to recognize the contribution of those people. And if that can reassure my colleague, I sincerely expect that by the end of February, the minister will have tabled in the House a bill that will provide exactly what he, I, all the committee members and, hopefully, all the members of this House and all Canadians want: that is to recognize the contribution of merchant seamen.

Madam Speaker, I want to put on record some of my thoughts with regard to the members of the merchant marine.
November 7, 1991

Routine Proceedings
A few Parliaments ago I had the honour of serving with the Hon. Daniel MacDonald who was then the Minister of Veterans Affairs. This topic of recognizing our merchant marines as we do our other veterans in Canada came up.
The former speaker mentioned that it has taken a long time to come around to the position where we recognize the sacrifice and the contribution made by the merchant marines. I and those who have served in this House are as much to blame as anyone for having procrastinated for so long.
I see today that there is agreement on all sides of this House. I have not heard anyone rise to oppose the recognition of the members of the merchant marines as we do our veterans with full honours and with full rights,
I might add.
My voice is added today to those of members who have spoken in favour of this recognition. Like the others I regret that it has taken so long. I am sure that the parliamentary secretary will advise the minister involved that there is concurrence in this House with the report before us.
To say that the merchant marines have made sacrifices on behalf of our country is truly sans dire. It goes without saying. Yet we have waited this long to grant them veterans' status. It just does not seem fair and it does not seem right.
I ask myself why, if merchant marines are eligible for medals, including other recognition such as prisoner of war allowances, that we in this House cannot grant them full recognition for what they have done? They can receive civilian war allowances equal in value to the War Veterans Allowances. However there is one thing they are not eligible for that should be corrected and it is the long-term care.
We know that merchant marines want access to the full range of programs offered to other status veterans. This is the very least we can do. They served for us on these merchant ships which for the most part were unarmed. They were able in one ship to carry enough food to feed almost a quarter of a million people for a full week. They made these hazardous crossings of the Atlantic numerous times and they did not even have guns to defend themselves. They were more or less at
the mercy of the U-boat packs which stalked them in the North Atlantic.
I ask myself why, if our allies, England, the United States and Australia have recognized the value of their merchant marines have we waited so long to recognize ours. Some of our veterans, for example, the Hong Kong veterans and the Dieppe prisoners were given extra recognition in the sense that we were able to get extra money and services for them. They deserved it because of the hurt and harm which they suffered at the hands of the enemy when they were taken prisoners of war.
In this House today, I see members who were on the veterans affairs committee when we had veterans from Hong Kong appear before us.
I cannot speak for them because they will take the floor in their own good time to tell of their experiences. I for one found it very difficult not to at least try to put myself in the shoes of these men who were taken prisoner and treated in such a shameful fashion.
They came to us, the government, for the services they needed because of what had been done to them on our behalf and because they were fighting for us during the war. I did not see how we could turn down their request. We did not turn down their request. We gave them what they wanted and what they needed at that time.
The only difference between the merchant marines and our other veterans, it seems to me, is that the merchant marines did not have uniforms on when they were fighting. They fought in the clothes that they wore day in and day out as they braved the hazards of the sea on our behalf. I do not think the uniform makes the man, but I can tell you that the man or the woman inside the uniform is what gives the honour and glory to the uniform which is worn.
Merchant ships in their effort to supply troops, found themselves in combat situations for which they were very ill equipped. I mention that in passing. Not only were they unarmed, but the U-boats that stalked and attacked them knew they were unarmed. I do not mean this as a pun but they were sitting ducks out in the water. Although they were carrying the majority of the supplies to our allies in England and elsewhere that were under siege, they themselves did not have the means to fight back.

November 7, 1991
Routine Proceedings
It has been said here in this House many times that the conditions under which they had to live and fight were many times more deplorable than situations for our other veterans. That is not to say that the other veterans had not served well. It is to recognize that all our merchant marines were able to perform under not only the most hazardous conditions but under conditions which even our other veterans in many cases did not have to face.
We take a look at their losses and see that proportionately they suffered losses which were higher than others. Permit me to enter into the record some of the facts about the merchant marines.
When the Second World War broke out our merchant navy consisted of only 37 ships and 1,400 personnel. But by the end of the war the numbers had increased to over 180 ships and 12,000 personnel. For those who say they do not know who these 12,000 merchant marines were, I say it is very easy to find out who they were because there were logs not only on the ships but there were records kept. These people would be very simple to recognize.
During the course of the war more than 70-and I repeat that, more than 70-Canadian ships were lost and the merchant mariners suffered losses which were in excess of those of the other forces. The pro rata losses of the merchant navy for the period 1939 to 1945 exceeded those of the Royal Canadian Navy by 40 per cent. I say that was due to the fact that they could not defend themselves as the others could. The over-all death rate in the merchant marine was about 9.55 per cent, compared to 3.98 per cent for the three armed forces.
In addition to these casualties, 198 were taken prisoners of war and spent an average of four years in prisoner of war camps, a period which was in many instances much longer than for any of the other services.
In 1983 I again had the honour to represent Canada at Vimy on November 11, I guess almost eight years ago from the date on which I am speaking now. Many veterans came with us to Vimy and we toured not only the cemeteries but some of the battlefields where our Canadian forces were involved. It was mentioned to me at that time by a veteran of the Royal Canadian Navy that we should recognize what the merchant mariners had done for us. It sort of stuck in my mind that here we
were honouring the Canadian dead of two world wars and now not one of the delegation who was there was from the merchant marines.
One of the members who spoke previously said that he had visited a cemetery in Yokohama. I believe this is close to where many of our Canadian soldiers who were taken prisoner at Hong Kong were interned during the war. They were buried there.
It might be a revelation for you and other members in this House to know that the merchant marine was very much involved on D-Day, on June 6. We had supply ships which were not right at the forefront but close enough within shelling range that they took casualties. I can attest that behind Juno Beach where our Canadian troops landed we have a Canadian cemetery and in that Canadian cemetery are members of the merchant marines.
I find it ludicrous that after all of these years these men who served side by side with our other forces and are buried with them do not have the same recognition as the others do. It is high time that we in the House of Commons and hopefully the minister who is in charge will recognize the great contribution that they made.
The motto of Canada's merchant mariners was: "We deliver the goods", and they did deliver the goods. They delivered them to England which at the time was under siege. I guess it could be said that England truly was under siege from 1939 well into 1944 when the allied troops were able to attack the bastion fortress Europe.
Where do you think all the supplies came from? How do you think the supplies got to our fighting troops? How is it that our brave men and women who were involved in the onslaught against fortress Europe were able to push our enemies back into the heartland of Europe and then finally defeat them? Where do you think those supplies came from? I say to you that those supplies were carried by our merchant mariners, the unsung heroes of the Second World War.
It was mentioned earlier that it took us quite a bit of time to strike a medal for Korean veterans. That too adds, if not to our shame, at least to our lack of recognition of the brave men and women who went to the battlefields to represent us. I think that the merchant mariners have waited long enough. I believe their due,
November 7, 1991

their right is to be recognized as full-fledged veterans of our armed forces.
The committee, as is stated here, believes that the Government of Canada should follow these recommendations and so do I. Canadian merchant marines with one or more high seas ocean going assignments during wartime should be fully recognized as veterans. Veterans' benefits should be extended to them without any exception. A book of remembrance that we would have here in the Peace Tower in Canada, and that I encourage all members to visit, should be prepared and placed in the Peace Tower. It should be solely dedicated to merchant mariners who died in Canada's wars.
The Department of Veterans Affairs should encourage the construction of a suitable monument to honour the memory of Canada's wartime merchant mariners. The committee suggested that Halifax would be a suitable area for the monument. From the information that I have about Halifax, the fact is that most of our supplies were shifted into Halifax and then transported to our friends and allies overseas.
Lest there be any question that members on all sides of this House are in agreement with this report and lest there be any doubt by the minister that we want action to be taken on behalf of the merchant mariners, I add my voice to those of my colleagues in my party as well as the members who have spoken from the NDP and the government to let it be known that our party categorically supports the inclusion of our merchant mariners as full-fledged veterans to be accorded all the honours and rights due to any and all veterans of the Canadian forces.

As a Canadian I find it very hard to accept that our young men were sent over there with the full knowledge that they were perhaps going to be getting the worst end of the deal when it came down to a battle for Hong Kong. Yet it was done.
The treatment they received at the hands of the Japanese is no less shameful than the decision to send them there in the first place. Some 45 years since the end of the Second World War, 46 years now, there has been some recognition by the Japanese government of the crimes, and I use the word purposefully, that the Japanese committed against our Canadians and the way they treated them as prisoners of war. I believe there should be compensation. There should be at least as much compensation from the Japanese for the way they treated Canadians as from us for the way we treated our Japanese Canadians who were here. We had no right to do that either.
It should be brought back to committee for discussion so that overtures can once again be made to the Japanese government to have it reconsider the fact that there should be compensation for the way our prisoners were treated at their hands.

I think I can say that every member of this House has the utmost admiration for Canada's merchant seamen. It has been mentioned by members that so many times throughout those dreadful war years they were merely sitting ducks while the U-boats stalked the convoys. Routine Proceedings
Much has been made about what our merchant mariners are not receiving. We have been hearing that all morning. I think it is only right that the Canadian public also learn about what our merchant mariners are receiving. It is certainly not chicken feed. This year alone merchant mariners and their dependents will be receiving something like $20 million worth of benefits and all of it is indexed and tax free.
It is illuminating to recall a statistic given by the member for Regina-Lumsden in his speech last Friday. He told the House that of the 12,000 merchant seamen who served their country in the Second World War about 3,500 are still living.
Veterans affairs indicates that over 3,000 claims from merchant seaman were processed just last year. This suggests that merchant seaman are getting very fair treatment from veterans affairs in many ways and that our present legislation is wide enough for the country to assist virtually all merchant seamen who come before veterans affairs with a claim for their benefits.
In contrast, it is worth noting that about one-third of all Canadian veterans are clients of veterans affairs.
I will talk a little about the programs that fuel this $20 million pay-out and will give a few examples of how individuals are benefiting. First, there is the allowance program which gives merchant mariners in financial difficulties income support and health care benefits.
Dependents are also eligible as are survivors of veterans.
The allowance program treats veterans and merchant seamen equally. I think it is important for us to emphasize that fact. It has done so since 1962.
This program involves not only money, but eligible merchant mariners can also receive health care benefits not covered by provincial programs. Eye glasses are covered, as are prescription drugs, dental care, hearing aids and chronic care in a community bed. The only benefit available to ex-military personnel and not to the civilian groups is access to a department or contract bid.
The allowance program is one of the reasons that Canada's programs and benefits are admired and envied by veterans in innumerable other countries. I point this out because we have heard how the United Kingdom regards its merchant mariners as veterans. That may be but the United Kingdom does not have an income

support program for merchant mariners or veterans as we do here in Canada.
The Royal Canadian Legion said in its submission to our House Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs: "The name 'veteran' without access to the benefits is very cold comfort indeed". The Veteran's Memorial Manor is a success story in itself, and because it is called the Veteran's Memorial Manor most Canadians would naturally assume that only veterans are housed there, but this gentleman is a former merchant mariner. subsubtopic: THE SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE ON THE GOVERNMENT OF CANADA'S PROPOSALS FOR A RENEWED CANADA-EXPENSES OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE NOT SITTING ON COMMITTEE-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
I am now ready to rule on the question of privilege raised on Wednesday, October 30, 1991, by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead. This matter relates to the expenses incurred by members of the House who were not members of that committee accompanying the Special Joint Committee on the Government of Canada's Proposals for a Renewed Canada to Prince Edward Island and Toronto. In this particular instance, the committee decided to pay the expenses of these members.
I would like to thank the hon. member for raising this matter and I would also like to express my appreciation to those members who intervened, namely the hon. government House leader and the hon. members for Winnipeg Transcona, Shefford, and Ottawa-Vanier. Their comments have been very helpful to the Chair in reviewing this incident.

In his intervention the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead argued that his role as a member in the House and in committee should not be dictated or appear to be dictated or influenced by the arbitrary rulings of the steering committee. In his opinion the action of the special joint committee in effect set up two classes of members in the House: on the one hand, the committee members and those members who were not members of the committee but who could follow the proceedings of the committee outside Ottawa and have their expenses paid for by the committee and, on the other hand, members who were not members of the committee and would have to seek the approval of its steering committee to have their expenses reimbursed if they wish to travel with the committee.

The hon. member questioned the legitimacy of the expenses incurred by the special joint committee in
paying the expenses of members of the House accompanying the committee but who were not members of the committee. These points were supported most ably by the hon. member for Shefford.

In his comments the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona quite rightly pointed out that in ruling after ruling I and other Speakers have determined that these kinds of interventions are matters which are properly dealt with by the committee itself. He also stated that the committee had made arrangements in order to do its job properly and in the context of its own authority and that the matter should not properly be before the House since the committee is its own master in this respect.

As noted at the time, I listened with some concern to the statement made by the hon. Member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead and agreed to take the matter under advisement.
Particularly troubling to the Chair was the suggestion that all members of this House were not being afforded equal treatment in this affair. This situation arose out of a problem with the membership of the committee which was first drawn to my attention by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead on September 25, 1991. In its ruling of September 27, 1991, the Chair found merit in the case made by the hon. member and directed that steps be taken to correct the situation.
On October 30, 1991, the 14th report of the Standing Committee on House Management was concurred in by the House and the full membership of the committee was established.

In the meantime however the special joint committee pursuant to its order of reference of June 19, 1991, proceeded with its work and in so doing made the administrative arrangements it deemed appropriate to carry out its mandate.
Having reviewed the matter, I must now reaffirm my initial view that this is a complaint over an administrative matter recommended by the steering committee and approved by the committee and should not have been submitted to the Chair.
November 7, 1991



As I noted in rulings on June 16, 1988, and December 18, 1989, we have a longstanding tradition in the House and there are many judgments to this effect, that unless something truly extraordinary should occur in committee, the committee is master of its own destiny. According to our traditions and practices, the Chair does not intervene with the proceedings of a committee unless a problem has been reported by the committee to the House or in extremely unusual circumstances.
The special joint committee has acted within the boundaries granted to it by its order of reference and hon. members can raise with the committee complaints they may have about the soundness of its administrative arrangements.
Finally, while reiterating our practice that committees are masters of their own procedure, I would remind all members that committees have the responsibility to conduct their affairs to ensure that complaints such as this do not arise, and that such matters, unless they relate to extreme situations where a Speaker would be required to intervene, should not take up the time of the House.
