speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to submit to the House for second reading Bill C-31, an act to amend the Extradition Act respecting appeals.
As members will know, Canadians are very concerned about our extradition laws. Several recent high profile cases have raised a concern in their minds that Canada, a country with an international reputation for safety and absence of crime, may be becoming a haven for criminals fleeing charges or punishment in other countries.
The source of much of this concern lies in the procedures currently available for appealing the decision of a judge in an extradition hearing and for reviewing the decision of the minister whether to surrender the fugitive to the foreign state.
The existing procedures, which I will outline in a moment, allow numerous appeals from both of these decisions, all of which can reach the Supreme Court of Canada on more than one occasion.
In addition, our international reputation has suffered among states with which we have agreed, through extradition treaties, to return wanted persons. The theories that those fleeing from justice in other countries
November 7, 1991

will attempt to enter Canada chiefly because our extradition laws are so complex that they can expect years of safe haven for the proceedings of their removal unfold.
Canadians will not permit their country to become a haven for fugitives. It is equally important however that our extradition laws be fair. Those charged with offences elsewhere should have an adequate opportunity to challenge the evidence brought forward by the requesting state.
It must not be forgotten that extradition applies not only to the return of foreigners, but also Canadian citizens to foreign lands where legal systems, language and culture may differ.
Further, we must ensure that Canada does not involve itself in the surrender of those who have fled other countries because of persecution on the grounds of race, religion or political belief or who, for whatever reason, will not be treated fairly on return.
We must also be confident that the person will be treated fairly and humanely upon his or her return. The judiciary ensures that there is solid foundation for the charges, and the minister ensures that the person surrendered will be treated fairly in the foreign state.
This bill strikes the proper balance between prompt return of wanted persons and protection for the person sought.

Under the present law, a state with which we have concluded an extradition treaty can ask Canada to turn over to it an accused person or offender of that state who is in Canada.
That person is then arrested and a legal investigation is conducted on the basis of the charge or on the reasons to believe that the person fled after being sentenced for an infraction committed on the territory of the requesting state.
During that investigation, a judge of a superior court or a provincial or territorial county court examines the evidence put forward and decides whether or not to detain the person sought until he or she is sent back to the requesting state.
If the accused person or offender is ordered to await extradition, he can request a writ of habeas corpus
Government Orders
challenging the decision of the extradition judge. At this stage, he can exercise all the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the charter and bring the matter to court. The decision of the judge who ruled on the habeas corpus can be appealed to the provincial or territorial court of appeal and this court's decision can be appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada with the latter's permission.
If the extradition judge does not order the person to be turned over to requesting state, it can appeal directly to the Supreme Court of Canada with the latter's permission.

Once this part of the procedure is completed, the minister considers any submissions made by the person sought with respect to humanitarian grounds, questions of fairness and such issues as whether the person would be facing the death penalty in the foreign state.
When the minister considers that the person should be extradited, a surrender warrant will be issued by the minister. The minister's decision with respect to surrender can also be judicially reviewed. That decision can in turn be appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal and with leave of the court to the Supreme Court of Canada.
This system is obviously enormously complex, results in long delays and requires a great deal of costly court time. The person's remedies far exceed those available to a person charged with a criminal offence under Canadian law.
In developing a more streamlined appeal and review system I have been guided by the following principles. First, the appeal and review process of extradition matters should resemble as nearly as possible the remedies available to those charged with criminal offences in Canada. Second, the person whose extradition is sought should enjoy the protections of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Third, to the extent possible, duplication of proceedings should be avoided.
The appeal and review process should be expedient but permit a fair hearing. The division of functions between the judiciary and the minister must be clearly respected. Our international obligations to our extradition treaty partners to return offenders must also be respected.

November 7, 1991
Government Orders
Taking these principles into account, Bill C-31 adopts the following approach.

Applications for extradition will always be brought to superior courts or provincial or territorial county courts.
Nevertheless, the extradition judge can now know the recourse under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms that may apply to the duties he is required to perform in applying this law.
Under the present law, charter issues may only be raised before the judge, usually on the same court as the extradition judge who received the writ of habeas corpus pursuant to the extradition request.
This results in needless duplication of administering evidence and wastes the courts' time. This change would allow charter-based arguments concerning applications to be considered at a later stage of the proceedings, without having to go before a different judge.
Charter-based arguments relating to the minister's extradition decision can be considered when the minister's decision is reviewed.

The bill allows the fugitive or the requesting state to appeal the decision of the extradition judge directly to the provincial or territorial court of appeal on grounds similar to those available to parties to criminal proceedings under the Criminal Code of Canada. The court of appeal is obliged under the bill to schedule the appeal hearing at an early date. In most cases, the minister will be obliged to make a decision whether to surrender the fugitive within 90 days of the committal of the fugitive at the extradition hearing.
Where there is an appeal by the fugitive from the committal the court of appeal can defer the appeal proceedings until the minister has made a decision on surrender. In cases where the legal issues are particularly complex, the minister can postpone the decision on surrender until the court of appeal has made its decision. However, in most cases the minister will make the decision on surrender before any appeal concerning the extradition judge's committal order is heard by the court of appeal.
Since the bill provides that judicial reviews from the minister are to go to the provincial and territorial courts of appeal, appeals from the extradition judge and judicial reviews from the minister's decision will usually be heard together. This will ensure that appeals and reviews will be conducted as expeditiously as possible since all issues will be dealt with together before a single court. Further, it will ensure that in extradition matters there will usually be only one subsequent avenue of recourse, the Supreme Court of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in order to speed up the process, the bill provides time limits.
The person sought can apply to the minister as soon as the extradition process begins and has up to 30 days following the detention order to do so; the minister can always consider these applications outside the time limit, if necessary.
The person sought or the requesting state must file a notice of appeal within 30 days of the decision.
The minister too must act within certain time limits.
As was said, normally the minister will decide whether to turn the person over within 90 days of the detention order.
There is an exception to the 90-day deadline in cases where the person sought has appealed the detention order and the minister wishes to wait for the appeal court's decision before ruling on the matter, given the complexity of the points of law that it raises.
In such cases, the minister can make his or her decision within 45 days of the appeal court's ruling.

The other exception is where the minister has received submissions from the fugitive with respect to surrender. As has been seen in some recent cases, these submissions can be lengthy and detailed. They may require the minister to conduct inquiries into the legal system or political climate in the requesting state or seek assurances from the requesting state with respect to the treatment of the fugitive upon return.
As such, the bill allows the minister to extend the 90-day period for one additional period of 60 days where necessary to act on the fugitive's submissions.

	
November 7, 1991

The bill contains a time limit within which a fugitive must be surrendered and a means of enforcing the time limit by which the minister is bound. Where the minister has not made a decision within the applicable time period the fugitive may apply for a writ of habeas corpus and is entitled to be released if the minister cannot show sufficient cause for the delay.
The same is true if the fugitive has not been removed from the country within the period of 45 days after the minister has made a surrender order, or after the completion of appeals from such an order.
In total the bill will remove the necessity for three steps: habeas corpus review, review by the Federal Court trial division, and Federal Court of Appeal.
Appeals from the extradition hearing and review of the minister's decision will be combined before the provincial court of appeal. Canada will be able to deal with extradition requests more promptly while at the same time offering protection to those sought by foreign countries. Our commitments to our extradition treaty partners can be honoured better. Most important, the signal will be sent to offenders abroad that they can no longer shield themselves from answering charges or serving a sentence by taking advantage of outdated Canadian extradition laws.
We have all seen the concern of Canadians over the past few years about the process of extradition as it related to the cases of Joseph Kindler and Charles Ng. There is absolute incomprehension on the part of many Canadians about why it would take so long, more than six years of due process, for the legal system of Canada to make a decision, yes or no, as to whether it was fair to extradite these individuals.
The complex appeal process meant that the first court to hear the question could not deal with the charter issues. Therefore charter issues had to be raised in the second court, and a full range of appeals made to the Supreme Court of Canada. Then the minister makes a decision, then the minister's decision is open to appeal to the Federal Court trial division, the Federal Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Canada. This is an enormously complex set of due process.
In the case of Charles Ng, when the second round of appeals started, the appeal of my predecessor's decision
Government Orders
to the Federal Court, I immediately referred the decision to the Supreme Court of Canada where the Kindler case was being examined in order to expedite the consideration of those cases. However clearly that recourse is not available to ministers in all cases. What we need is substantive structural change in our law.
I am putting before the House in Bill C-31 a simplification which does not remove any of the rights of the fugitive. It is up-to-date, modem legislation taking into account the need to hear charter arguments in the court of first instance, taking into account the need of ministers to respond quickly and to make decisions by imposing time limits on them, taking into account the efficiency of hearing appeals from a minister's decision and from an extradition judge in the same process in the court of appeal where appropriate.
All of these will help to reassure Canadians that this country will not become a haven for fugitives from foreign countries because of the laxity or inefficiency of our law. It will also ensure that people will not be able to evade justice in other countries because of long, extended delays of due process here which make it almost impossible to pursue prosecutions in the requesting country because of the aging of evidence, the death of witnesses and the inability of prosecutors to keep a case alive.
This is very important legislation that all Canadians will be able to relate to directly. Therefore I move:
That Bill C-31, an act to amend the Extradition Act be referred
to the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak about the extradition law. I am sure that people are glued to their TV sets to hear all of the exciting discussion about extradition. It is kind of a dry subject but it does have very serious ramifications for our communities and the safety of Canadians in general. For that reason alone it is a pleasure to speak.
This has been a week of justice and law and order issues. The tragedy about what is taking place with all of this legislation, including extradition but also corrections reform, the mental disorder legislation, young offenders and gun control is that we have a situation where the government is reacting rather than providing leadership. It is reacting to things that have occurred outside when it should have already anticipated them and done something.
The mental disorder legislation is a clear example of one law which the government knew for three or four years was deficient and had to be corrected. It knew that it had problems with the young offenders legislation but that has been slow in coming forward. Again it knew there were problems with this legislation, it knew what it was dealing with in the recent decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada. We are seeing a reactive government rather than a government providing leadership.
Everything is done in phases. We do not take a holistic point of view with regard to crime prevention or even a holistic view as far as specific pieces of legislation are concerned. In this particular bill we are dealing with a phase. We are also dealing with phases in parole reform because we are looking at sentencing. We still have to look at the detention provisions for young offenders. The mental disorder legislation requires that we wait for three years until hospital orders are dealt with and we see how those are going to work.
It occurs over and over. All we are doing is phasing things rather than dealing with the whole bill or with the whole issue. I am afraid that most Canadians would really like to see us phase out this government and get on with some leadership.
Right on. Get rid of them.

My colleague confirms that insightful comment of mine.
As I said before, extradition is a dry topic. The old law has been in existence since 1877. In most cases, extradition is a treaty between nations. The intent of extradition is to secure the return of Canadian fugitives and rid the country of its foreign criminals. Gerard La Forest, before he was on the Supreme Court of Canada, made that comment in one of his treatises on extradition.
Our law is outmoded. It is old legislation. The treaties in a lot of cases are old. It is a veiy complicated procedure. The minister already outlined the back and forth movements through the different appeal procedures which have to occur. We know that it does not work. We have seen that this type of appeal approach plays into the hands of the fugitive who is in our country and at the same time provides no benefit to our citizens.
In fact it creates a very heavy cost. If you accept that it costs about $70,000 a year to keep somebody incarcerated, in the Ng case we have had this fugitive from the United States in our country for six years. It probably cost us upwards of $500,000 for that one person, and that does not even include the costs for lawyers, appeals and judges.
In the maritimes lawyers are very inexpensive but Ontario solicitors are very expensive. That adds even further cost to an already expensive procedure.
You get what you pay for.

There is no question you get what you pay for. That is why it takes six years to get rid of somebody like Ng with Ontario solicitors.
The Ng case and the Kindler case are two cases which we really should take a look at because they were abuses of the system.
Charles Ng was wanted in California on 12 counts of murder and he also faced sexual assault and torture charges. He fled to Calgary in 1985 and was convicted for an armed robbery. It has taken us from 1985 until now to see him returned to California. Some will say that he should not even have been sent back because of the death penalty and the issues associated with that.
November 7, 1991

In my view, and I think the view of most Canadians, he was a fugitive in our country who should have been returned to his country to face the judicial system there.
We must have some concerns with countries where penalties associated with the crimes are so serious that we wonder whether there is in fact justice in those countries. That is the type of situation where we may want to consider not sending back fugitives who are in our country. Obviously the United States has a justice system which pursues justice. In the United States there is fairness and equality as best it can be delivered by any justice system.
In that case and the Kindler case with the number of appeals to courts and appeals to provinces and then to the Supreme Court of Canada, I do not believe their rights have been violated. That is exactly what the United States said.
Again I quote Mr. Justice La Forest when he wrote for the majority: "This court has held that extradition must be refused if surrender would place the fugitive in a position that is so unacceptable as to shock the conscience of Canadians. But I do not think that the surrender of fugitives who may ultimately face the death penalty abroad would, in all cases, shock the conscience of Canadians". I would certainly agree with that position. It was a wise decision on the part of the Supreme Court of Canada.
We are maybe going to see the process speeded up when this legislation is done. We are going to see this again in the Bembenek case, back and forth, appeals and more appeals.
We agree with the government's approach that we must streamline the system. We must make it more efficient.
We are going to support this bill going to committee. We are going to seek the advice of counsels who deal with this particular law and seek the counsel of all who have come in contact with it so that they can advise us as to whether there are more efficient ways to streamline this particular legislation. It still is a situation where you have in effect two lines that ultimately end up at the Supreme Court of Canada. In our view there may be methods arrived at by the justice committee under the
Government Orders
able leadership of the hon. member for Mississauga West. He has provided a lot of recommendations to the minister on extradition but has had no success in convincing the minister of the wisdom that came from that committee.
This particular legislation does not fully deal with all of the recommendations that came out of the justice committee report. There is still the two-track judicial executive process. There are still ongoing negotiations between Canada and the United States. We are still going to have to proceed with more negotiations, more treaties. The minister in earlier comments has indicated that there are still 30 other areas within this whole ambit of extradition that have to be dealt with and that this bill only deals with one aspect. These areas include evidentiary provisions, the minister's discretion and non-treaty extradition and judicial authority, to name just a few.
There is a lot of work to be done. This government is only dealing with one aspect of it and not really proceeding in a holistic manner. This is a situation where we can provide security and safety for our residents, and also not put this country through the very extensive costs associated with keeping fugitives in our system and running up and down through our court system for six years.
The abuses of our system cannot be allowed to continue. I know that you are concerned about that, Mr. Speaker. Canadians are concerned about it. For that reason we are supportive of the legislation going forward.
We are also concerned that Canada could become a safe haven for criminals fleeing any other jurisdiction and particularly the United States, because that is where a lot of cases have emanated from.
There is no question that we here on this side of the House do not want to see Canada become a safe haven for criminals fleeing any jurisdiction. That is exactly what Ng did. He knew or felt that he could safely come to Canada and because of our existing system it would be a safe place to hide, but also if he was caught it would be a good system to abuse so that he would not have to go back to California and face the music he would have to face. As a result, he had a free lunch in our country for six years. That is what we are opposed to.
Let us proceed with this legislation, let us get the advice and we will deal with it. We recognize it is a

November 7, 1991
Government Orders
piecemeal legislation only dealing with certain aspects. We are urging the government to examine crime prevention, safety in our communities, and that whole issue, and to deal with it all as one major issue. Instead we are forced because the government sets the agenda to look at band-aid solutions and half hearted legislation. It is all over the waterfront as far as what is needed in our communities.
We must deal with the basic issue of safety and protection in our communities. This legislation really will not do that much to help because there is so much more that needs to be done. In any event it is legislation which we will support as far as going to committee. I am pleased that it is going to the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General where there is a degree of expertise.
We have already made recommendations in the area of extradition and so the expertise that is available will be brought to bear on this particular legislation. I am sure that we will see it improved before it comes back to the House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise as justice critic for the New Democratic Party to speak on this legislation. We have called for this for a long time.
The Supreme Court ruled 4 to 3 that you could. There is the Ng case and the Leonard Peltier case-remember that case, Mr. Speaker-which was about a decade ago now. Mr. Peltier is still in jail in the United States. He is a native leader of the American Indian movement from the United States who was extradited.
The member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, Mr. All-mand, who is the former Solicitor General said that Mr. Peltier was extradited on false evidence. He was extradited on fabricated affidavits that were thrown out quickly by Canadian authorities. I think we extradited Mr. Peltier wrongly from Canada. That is believed now.
We have the Ng case on the one hand and the Peltier case on the other hand. One is too slow and the other is too quick, where we made a mistake. I think we have to have a fair procedure so we do not make any mistakes.
The other thing we have to do is be less hypocritical, if I may say so, and more honest in these particular cases. We have to have a single standard and not a double standard. Let me give you this example.
Peter Worthington, the noted journalist and the fellow who ran for this Parliament unsuccessfully, is now taking up the case of Lawrencia Bembenek, Bambi. You have Charles Ng on the one hand who is an accused mass murderer and let me put it this way, he is not in. any sense of the word an attractive personality.
We support the bill in principle but we are concerned that it is somewhat of a knee jerk reaction. Let me explain why. We have to find a balance in terms of extradition.
If you look at the Charles Ng case, which my friend who last spoke just mentioned, the accused mass murderer from California was in jail in Canada and exhausted the appeals procedure in Canada.
You have Ng on the one hand who people like Mr. Worthington and backbenchers in the Conservative Party over there would just deal with in a minute. On the other hand, you have Bambi. Bambi happens to be in certain ways of describing it, an attractive individual although-
What has that got to do with it?

You wonder what it has to do with it. There seems to be a double standard about it.
Without understanding all the intricacies of the law on extradition, people understood that was too long. Charles Ng was in the province of Alberta in jail. That seemed too long for a decision as to whether or not he should be extradited. There was a special reason why it was wrong. They were testing the case in the Supreme Court of Canada and the principle of whether you could extradite someone back to another country that had the death penalty when we do not have the death penalty in Canada.
Suddenly, the Bambi case has a lot to know, so maybe we are moving too fast in that sort of case. That is a case in which a woman was convicted in the United States of a murder. She came to Canada and is fighting extradition in Canada.
I have no comment on the case at all except to say there is a bit of a double standard here between the way people were writing about Ng and the way they are writing about Bambi.

What we have to do as MPs is write laws that work for everyone on extradition. That is why it is a very difficult subject.
I want to say first of all that one of the problems is the tone that the government has used on extradition, the tone that some of the backbenchers and the government party have used. I believe they are using the fallacy that Canada is about to become a haven for criminals from other countries because of our allegedly lax extradition laws.
This is simply not true. Also as was pointed out by some of the judges in the Kindler and Ng cases in the Supreme Court of Canada, there is no evidence of the existence or the threat of a flood of criminal fugitives pouring over our borders. Where is the evidence? In fact the number of requests received by Canada has remained consistently below 100 in the past five years. We got a breakdown from the Department of Justice from their annual report of the cases. I think the House would be interested in this.
In the period 1985 to 1986 the requests received from the United States for extradition were 69, from other countries, 14. You add them up, 69 and 14. We surrendered 23 people.
In 1986 to 1987 requests received from the United States were 47 and from other countries, 16. We surrendered 21.
In 1987 to 1988 there were 71 requests from the United States and 14 from other countries.
In 1988 to 1989 there were 64 requests from the United States and 12 from other countries. We surrendered 45.
In 1989 to 1990 there were 55 requests from the U.S. and 7 from other countries and we surrendered 39.
I managed to get the statistics for this year up to date,
1990-1991. We received 55 requests from the United States and 11 from other countries. We surrendered 55 people.
We are talking about 66 people to date.
This hardly makes Canada a haven for fugitives that are in our jails that are just there waiting to be extradited. I did add them up. This is not a big number. The member says add them up.
Government Orders
What is important is that the present time-consuming procedures be streamlined. That is why we agree with the bill. They should be streamlined. But we have to maintain at the same time procedural and substantive fairness and justice for the fugitive. I draw again the reference to the Peltier case where we extradited the fellow too quickly and wrongly.
The second problem we have here, and the previous speaker pointed this out although I do not think the minister pointed it out, is that the extradition treaties that we have with many countries are out of date. They date from the colonial period and contain archaic language.
Did you know that computer crime is not in most of the extradition treaties because they come from the 19th century when there were no computers. That is a big area. You can get into computer viruses and some of the thefts that occur as a result of computer crime. Consider that. It is not in the treaty and most of our treaties are old. There are a couple of modem treaties that have been affected. Let me just explain this for the members. In the old treaties they listed the crime, procuring an abortion for example. There were some wild old crimes that are no longer crimes in Canada. The new modem treaties just say a crime with over one year, for example, imprisonment. It is a very flexible list of crimes then.
We do not have modern treaties with very many countries and that definitely is a problem.
There is also a case now before the Supreme Court of Canada where the court will have to deal with the question of whether it is necessary that a defence be named in both treaties before it becomes extraditable.
Another possible amendment that the Minister of Justice could look at in dealing with this whole matter of extradition would be to undertake that the death penalty would not be carried out if the fugitive were extradited. We do not apply the death penalty in Canada and we may want to talk about that with other countries.
I am afraid we are going to have cases not like Charles Ng which was such an obvious case but we will have other cases where we pass a quick law with quick extradition where we could have real injustice. Good law is not made by one case. You need a number of cases and you need to see the balance that is there.

November 7, 1991
Government Orders
Another question is the proposal that the fugitive only have 30 days to make submissions to the Minister of Justice after the decision is made that they are in fact extraditable and we may want to extend that.
One of the problems noted by Mr. Bob Anderson, who is appearing for the Canadian Bar Association, is that the Court of Appeal normally does not hear direct evidence. This would limit the ability of the fugitive to present a full defence as can be done at present.
In an interview in the French press, Mr. Anderson said:

The new procedure will be shorter, but lawyer Robert Anderson was nevertheless afraid it might cause a number of complications, because the Court of Appeal will in some respects have to take the place of the Federal Court and the Superior Court. He is particularly concerned that one could appeal directly to the provincial Court of Appeal on all matters-extradition, incarceration and the ministers' decision-without first going through another court.

So Mr. Anderson is drawing attention to a problem with the present government proposals and perhaps we could hear the Canadian Bar Association in the committee.
I want to say just a little bit more about the notion that computer crime is not an extradictable offence between Canada and most of the countries with which we have extradition treaties.
I mentioned that there is some old law in there where you could extradite someone who was charged with procuring a miscarriage and so on and there are a lot of old parts of law.
In the limited time I have left let me just deal with some of the new treaties and explain them Mr. Speaker. Recently, Canada has begun signing treaties with such countries as India and the Netherlands, which get around the problem of not having named the crime on a list. They do this by making extradictable any crime which is punishable by more than one year in prison. This covers both computer crime sections but there are dozens of other treaties which will have to be replaced before the question is comprehensively covered.
The extradition treaty with the United States is a special case. The existing treaty was ratified in 1976 but
there is an updated version that has been ratified in Canada. This is the question I was going to put to the minister, before the government rather rudely nixed that question. I was not trying to exploit a minister of the House, I was going to ask a legitimate question. The question was: What is the state of the new extradition treaty with the United States? It is absolutely fundamental to this debate.
I believe that the American Senate is apparently holding up approval at their end and I stand to be corrected by any government member who will deal with this. This has caused a problem in the case of a Quebec truck driver, Richard Bilodeau. He was charged with manslaughter in the highway deaths of two New Hampshire state troopers and their prisoner. He was in jail in New Hampshire on a $500,000 bail and there was some controversy over whether the existing extradition treaty would enable the Americans to get Bilodeau back if he was allowed to return to Canada. So the judge did not want to give him bail, and poor Mr. Bilodeau had to sit in jail for a long time. Finally he did get released.
Initially the judge held that the Extradition Act and treaty would enable Bilodeau to avoid returning to the United States. Finally bail was set for this man. This is an unacceptable situation. You cannot put Canadians in this position. We have to clear up these treaties with the United States.
Although these new treaties will eliminate the anomaly of computer crimes not being extradictable offences, there does not seem to be any rush by the government to replace the ancient treaties now in place with most industrial countries. This leaves great scope for mischief, especially given the amount of damage which can be done to data banks using either the virus which affects computer systems through software or by direct tampering through illegal entry.
Anyway I do not have to run through these cases of computer hackers doing damage. All I want to do is point out that there is a real danger that valuable Canadian data could be tampered with or stolen or destroyed by some other country and under the state of our law and our treaties, we could do nothing about it. We could not extradite the person from there and they could not extradite the person from Canada.


I think this is a serious matter and needs to be looked at. Piracy on the Great Lakes is an extraditable offence, computer crime is not. I find that incredible. This bill is doing nothing to deal with that.
Let me just sum up our position on the bill again. Before I end my speech I want to set out for the government, if I might, some possible witnesses for the committee. I mentioned Mr. Anderson from the Canadian Bar Association. I would also suggest that we want to speak to Amnesty International which was involved in the events surrounding the Charles Ng extradition.
There are some allegations that we may have broken international law by the very quick reaction after the Supreme Court of Canada ruling. Mr. Ng was out of there in about two seconds flat. We want to hear some of that evidence. We might attempt to bring in groups like Victims of Violence, and also groups like Amnesty International.
The lawyer for Bambi Bembenek, Frank Morocco, whom I went to high school with in Toronto, could also be brought in to talk about the dangers of having a procedure which would whisk fugitives out of the country before the full facts of the case can be brought forward.
Another potential witness could be the lawyer for Mr. McVey and the case that I mentioned in the Supreme Court of Canada. We might also want to hear from Mr. Jardine, the crown counsel from Vancouver and perhaps Mr. David Gibbons, defence counsel, in the Inderjit Singh Reyat case. That was the man convicted of I believe it was manslaughter in the Air India matter, the bombing at Narita airport in Japan. There was a long fight on extradition on that case. I would like to hear some of the experience there.
This is not an open and shut matter. It is an area of many sides and many issues. Finally, I would like to hear Mr. Donald McLeod, the counsel for Charles Ng, who fought the extradition procedure I guess to the end.
The minister has summarized what the bill does. It does cut the number of steps. It used to go from an extradition hearing to a writ of habeas corpus, to an appeal to the relevant provincial court of appeal, appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada and then back to
Routine Proceedings
appeal the minister's decision to the Federal Court and then to appeal the Federal Court's decision to the Federal Court of Appeal and then to appeal it to the Supreme Court of Canada.
That was clearly too long. My friend from Peterborough whom I see over there brought in a private member's bill that was the opposite. It was too short and probably violated the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Has the government found the right balance? I hope so. The new legislation will have an extradition hearing. You will have an appeal to the relevant provincial court of appeal and then an appeal to the Supreme Court. The fourth and fifth steps are an appeal of the minister's decision to the provincial court of appeal and appeal that to the Supreme Court of Canada. That can be done concurrently.
We have a procedure that has very much speeded up the process. I hope it strikes the right balance. We will see that in committee. We have got to find somewhere between Ng on the one hand and Peltier on the other, between the way we approach Ng and other cases as we approach the Bambi case. We have got to try to deal with it rationally and we have to get a system that is fair.
We have to keep in mind that we still are talking about a relatively small amount of cases. People are not flooding into Canada to take advantage of weak extradition laws.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Ms. Campbell (Vancouver Centre) that Bill C-31, an act to amend the Extradition Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General.

Mr. Speaker, I heard the speakers who have entered this debate thus far and I would like to address a few questions to my colleague from Port Moody-Coquitlam. He seems to be quite taken with this computer crime and I am sure that we can put our minds together so that we get after these computer criminals. I would hope that would be addressed in the other sections they are going to be dealing with in their committee.
I came across a quote that I would like the hon. member to comment on, if he would. It is a quote from Mr. Justice Gerard La Forest. He says:
There can be no doubt that the appellant's right to liberty and security of the person is very seriously affected because he may face the death penalty following his return to the country he is going back to. The real question is whether surrender under these conditions violates the principles of fundamental justice.
I would like him to address himself to that part, and also:
The Supreme Court has held that extradition must be refused if surrender would place the fugitive in a position that is so unacceptable as to shock the conscience. But I do not think the surrender of fugitives who may ultimately face the death penalty abroad would in all cases shock the conscience of Canadians.
I would like him to give us his thoughts, if he would because I, for one, respect his thoughts very much in this
House and I would like him to comment on what Mr. Justice La Forest has to say about the "conscience of Canadians". Are we a nation such that it takes more than normal circumstances to shock us? Should we be returning these people at the earliest possible moment, especially in cases like the Ng case?

Thank you, it is a good question. What I was trying to do in my speech was to say we must be careful how we react. Sometimes one case can make bad law when we have got to look at it. I gave the example of the Ng case, in which it seemed obvious to the common sense of Canadians that this thing took too long. I think that is pretty obvious.
One of the reasons it took too long, I can say to the hon. member, is because the court was sorting out the very important legal issue of whether it should extradite someone back to a state that has the death penalty. That is one of the reasons it took too long. I will not comment on the court, it made its decision. It is the Supreme Court of Canada, and we live by that decision. The court ruled that you could send someone back to a state that has the death penalty. That is the law of Canada. I accept that.
What I was saying was we have to be careful. You look at the Ng case and you think we have got to get them out of here quickly, it is too long, and so on. It looks so obvious, but then you look back on our history and you look at the Peltier case and now as we get farther away from it, we look back and say that maybe we made a mistake there. We were so fast and we accepted affidavits that were not right. Now maybe we had better just be careful. If you just did it with the Peltier case you may have a whole different view of extradition.
I said also to look at the same commentators who at one moment, and I mentioned one journalist, want to get this Ng out of here fast and then suddenly Bambi comes along who is kind of a different figure and they say "wait a minute now we had better take our time and we had better look at this and we had better have lots of appeals, and why do we not let her out on bail, and why do we not do this?" I would not want to prejudice the case but I hope it works out justly, if I could put it that way.
That is what I am saying. I am saying just be careful which way you move. I cannot comment on what the judge said.

I respect the judge, and I agree with the ruling of the Supreme Court. It was a 4 to 3 ruling. Some judges differ.
The reason I mention computer crime was that I was trying to illustrate that there are two problems, not only the law but the issue of extradition treaties. We have some pretty old treaties through which you could get extradited for piracy on the Great Lakes, but you do not get extradited for computer crimes.
I think that is a bit strange and that is why I was mentioning it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Domm (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for Science):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two American fugitives were quietly whisked away to the United States on Thursday, September 27, 1991 within hours of the Supreme Court ruling that said they could be extradited even though they may face the death penalty. In a sharply divided 4-3 decision, the highest court in the land cleared the way to send Charles Ng to California where prosecutors want to charge him in at least a dozen sex/torture killings.
The Supreme Court also ruled that Joseph Kindler could be extradited to Pennsylvania where he has already been convicted of murdering a fellow criminal with a baseball bat. Last minute talk of appeals to the United Nations human rights committee that might have delayed extradition were rendered moot by the swift action of not only the justice minister for Canada, but of the federal justice authorities.
Within 30 minutes of the mid-morning release of the decision, a shackled and handcuffed Ng was handed over to a U.S. sheriff and flown from Prince Albert, Saskatchewan to Sacramento, California on an RCMP jet. Kindler left the country at 3 p.m. the day of the decision.
Ng later arrived at McLellan Air Force Base near Sacramento amid tight security. He was taken by a state
Government Orders
corrections department car to nearby Fulsom prison. Ng was to be kept separated from other inmates, a prison spokesman said. Ng was arraigned on September 27 in San Andreas, a small town in the Sierra Nevada about 240 kilometres east of San Francisco and 40 kilometres from the hideaway that he allegedly used to kill and torture his victims.
Ng's lawyer was outraged when he learned his client had been hustled on to a plane without being given an opportunity to contact him. Don MacLeod, Ng's lawyer, said at a news conference in Calgary: "To be perfectly honest with you, I am absolutely ashamed of my government and outraged at its conduct".
In interviews with the justice minister, she made no apologies for the speedy action. She went on to say: "There is a very strong sense of urgency to allow justice to take its course in the United States. Both men have been fighting extradition since 1985".
In the case of Mr. Ng, the case has not gone to trial. Witnesses are getting older, and witnesses are dying. I believe it was essential to act as quickly as possible after a careful review of the Supreme Court decision.
I compliment the minister on her quick decision to hand Ng over to U.S. authorities. I would also like to express my appreciation to the 185,000 people from across Canada who wrote in urging for speedy extradition of both of these people, Ng and Kindler.
I might also say that when it went through the justice committee, of which I am proud to say I was a member at that time, it gave a majority report. It was not only a majority report, it was a unanimous report from the justice committee that we proceed with extradition legislation. They presented the report to the minister at the time, who is the present Minister of Justice.
An investigation was launched by the former justice minister and he announced that to the United States when he attended a conference of legal persons in Washington. That body reported to the minister and I am pleased to say we had quick action.
As for the former speaker's statement that this bill before the House is all right and includes things that he would like to see, but it is not quite as fast a process as I was looking for, I suggest that he check my bill against the bill that is before the House. The reality of the situation is that the bill before the House today by the

Government Orders
justice minister and the Government of Canada is a speedier process than even my bill was.
To make this as easily understood as possible we have taken the legislation that we would like to enact and completely eliminated the two track system. Rather than going through a provincial court and then a Federal Court with all of the appeals following, we only go through the provincial court. We have taken the habeas corpus and put it into the hearing simultaneously with the provincial hearings. Also any conflicts the bill might have with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, for example, are dealt with now in that one track system through the provincial courts rather than Federal Court. There is no opportunity for anyone being extradited to move from the minister's signature for extradition to the Federal Court.
If this bill passes it will happen with one extradition hearing, one Superior Court appeal in the provincial courts and then possibly, if the Supreme Court deems it necessaiy on request, a third hearing before the Supreme Court. That is a guaranteed two hearings and a possible Supreme Court of Canada hearing. That speeds it up considerably compared to the former process where there were seven guaranteed hearings in the cases of Ng and Kindler. Those two cases followed the two track system.
I was pleased to see that the member of the NDP, who presented his view, is leaning toward passing this as quickly as we can because he feels that there need to be changes made. However I disagree with his logic that my bill would have given the fugitive fewer chances or more chances or whatever he intended to mean. That was not the fact because what he said is clearly contradicted by the facts.
The lawyer for Ng said he had filed a complaint with the UN human rights committee which had agreed to investigate Ng's case. He was told the committee asked Canadian authorities to hold off extradition until the investigation was complete. Our minister said she welcomed the views of the UN committee but felt extraditing the two was the proper course. Justice department officials do not believe the government would be legally bound by any UN ruling.
Officials at Amnesty International were holding a news conference appealing to the government to take
time to consider the ruling when they learned that Ng was already gone. Roger Clark, secretary general of the Canadian chapter of Amnesty International, said: "It seems to me that shows inappropriate and unseemly haste. I regret that the Canadian government has moved with such speed to support the possible execution of an individual".
Gary Rosenfeldt, founder of the lobby group Victims of Violence, headquartered in Ottawa welcomed the decision to send Ng and Kindler back to the United States. He said: "I really think that for the last number of years Canada has become a real haven for criminals". I would take his judgment of the haven that we have become ahead of the judgment, with respect, of my hon. friend from the New Democratic Party.
I would also like to point out with regard to Canada being a safe haven for criminals from the United States, the RCMP have information to indicate that when Ng was in prison in the United States he researched what was the best country in the world to escape to to avoid the death penalty. That would indicate to me that he chose Canada because it was the best. It probably means that we are the most lenient.
The same process occurred with Joseph Kindler. He escaped from the American prison where he was on death row using a set of bed sheets. I cannot quite figure out how he got out a window on death row, but that is the story that appeared in the media. He certainly got out of the prison. He escaped as quickly as he could to Canada, to safe haven, because his research showed that we have the most liberal laws in the world.
If that is not enough evidence I have letters from both the governor of the state and the Attorney General of the United States saying that we will turn Canada into a haven. Why would anyone not want to come to Canada under the best of circumstances and under the worst of circumstances?
If you were sentenced to be executed the best thing you could do would be to come to Canada and spend the rest of your days locked up in a prison cell rather than be executed. There is all kinds of documentation. Whether it is 2, 4 or 16 people who want to come to Canada does not make any difference to me. If one wants to come to Canada because our laws are the most liberal laws in the
November 7, 1991

world then we have to take a look at our laws to see if they really are the most liberal.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext:
You will have an opportunity to ask questions in just a few minutes.
Lawyers for both men had argued that the death penalty violates fundamental justice and amounts to cruel and unusual punishment, contrary to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. They wanted to force the justice minister to seek guarantees from California and Pennsylvania that they would not impose capital punishment if the two were returned.
Under the Canada-U.S. extradition treaty the federal justice minister can ask American authorities for such a guarantee. However none of the ministers who have held the justice portfolio over the last six years has made that request.
The court ruled it is not unconstitutional to return Ng and Kindler to a country that has a justice system similar to Canada's, with legal safeguards for the rights of the accused. However in a strongly worded dissent Justice Peter Cory called capital punishment: "The ultimate desecration of human dignity".
Ng, a Hong Kong native and one time U.S. marine, is wanted to face 18 charges, including 12 of murder, in connection with a series of kidnappings, torture and murders in northern California.
He avoided trial by fleeing to Calgary where he was arrested and convicted for shooting a store security guard in the hand during a bungled shoplifting attempt.
Kindler was convicted of beating an acquaintance to death with a baseball bat to keep the man from testifying against him in a burglary case in Philadelphia. The jury recommended the death penalty but Kindler escaped from jail before the sentence could be imposed and fled to Montreal where he was later arrested.
There have been no executions in Canada since 1962. Parliament formally abolished the death penalty in Canada in 1976 and rejected a move to restore it in 1987. Canada still has capital punishment for acts of treason. No death sentences have been carried out in Pennsylvania or California for acts of treason in more than two decades. I do not know how long it has been since we
Government Orders
executed anyone for acts of treason in Canada. I tried to research that but I could not find any.
If it resumed executing prisoners, Pennsylvania would do it by lethal injection. California formerly executed prisoners by gas.
When all was said and done the issue before the Supreme Court of Canada was: "Must Canada insist that a different free and democratic society, whose judicial system we otherwise accord equal status and trust as our own, fundamentally alter its view of what a fit sentence is for a certain crime?"
The root of the disagreement was the death penalty. In Canada the democratically elected representatives of the people decided not to allow capital punishment, while in California the democratically elected representatives of their people have decided to allow it. The lawyers arguing on behalf of Ng suggested that Canada should have imposed its will on California and that failure to do so constituted cruel and unusual punishment for Ng.
Canada's Minister of Justice refused to go along with this idea, citing six different basic premises for that decision in October 1989. The first was that constitutional safeguards within the United States' criminal and justice system to ensure standards of fairness are at least equal to our own. The second was a recognition that the request for no death penalty assurances are not sought routinely and the facts of the Ng case did not so require it.
The third was a rejection of the time on death row, if convicted, as being cruel and unusual punishment.
The fourth was a rejection of the method of execution in California as being cruel and unusual punishment.
The fifth was a rejection of the fact that Canada does not have the death penalty as dictating that we cannot extradite a fugitive to a country that does.
The sixth was if it was generally anticipated that by fleeing to Canada a person accused of capital murder could escape exposure to the death penalty it is foreseeable that Canada would become a safe haven for such criminals. In my view such a prospect is simply unacceptable.
Here are the two opinions. Opinion A on this issue is uphold the minister's decision and return Ng with no, assurances of no death penalty sought. The message from this decision is straightforward. If a person commits capital murder in the United States and then comes to

November 7, 1991
Government Orders
Canada and is caught and ordered extradited they will be sent back to face justice in their own jurisdiction. Canada will not be a safe haven for U.S. killers.
Opinion B on this issue is refuse to extradite unless California agrees to waive the death penalty.
Both district attorneys involved in the Ng case and the Joseph Kindler case, both heard by the Supreme Court at the same time, on February 21, 1991, stated in different ways but equally unequivocally, as Paul Cummings, the assistant district attorney for San Francisco said: "Canada is becoming a safe haven for killers from the United States".
Similarly assistant district attorney Richard DeBene-detto remarked in relation to the Kindler case that: "If they know they can go somewhere and possibly avoid the death penalty they are not going to hesitate". The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada on the Ng case will have profound effects on the domestic security of this country for years to come.
If the latter choice had been taken we automatically and realistically would have become a haven for fugitive killers seeking to avoid justice in the United States of America. To make it worse, if the United States had then refused to comply with our conditions not only would we be such a haven but we would already have our first beneficiaries of this policy in our midst, Charles Ng and Joseph Kindler.
I took a little time-am I already at 20 minutes? It must have been the interventions. One more minute, then.
Point of order.

speechtext: The hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam.
I would have no objections if the hon. member wishes to continue, provided he does not abuse it. I would like to hear him out. He has presented bills on this case.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Science
speechtext:
I really appreciate the help from the opposition in finishing my case.
I took some time and I sent this around to all colleagues in the House of Commons. It is my centrefold. It deals with the 4 to 3 vote when the Supreme Court of Canada decided that the two American fugitives could be extradited to face possible death sentences. I went to the core of the 100 or 200 pages that we received from the Supreme Court-if we paid $5 per package-on the decisions and the lead-up to the decisions that they made in the Ng and Kindler cases. I want members to listen to this because this might motivate me to do something about capital punishment. In section 12 of the charter it says that:
Everyone has the right not to be subjected to any cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. The death penalty deprives the prisoners of all vestiges of human dignity. If Kindler or Ng committed murder in Canada the provision of section 12 in the charter would prevent capital punishment.
I did not write that. It came from the Supreme Court of Canada, section 12. How did the Supreme Court rule on section 12? I will read that into the record. This is the majority view of the Supreme Court:
Much has been said and written in this country on the death penalty and there is no clear consensus in this country that capital punishment is morally abhorrent and absolutely unacceptable. Tb this day capital punishment continues to apply to certain military offences. Polls continue to show a considerable support among Canadians for the return of the death penalty for certain offences. Returning the fugitive to face capital punishment would not shock the Canadian consciences.
We are talking about a majority position of Canadians and I am talking about what could very well be a majority consensus in this House of Commons. I think there is room to consider as a private member's initiative, a bill for capital punishment for acts of terrorism causing loss of innocent life, whether it is the Air India accident or some other such accident. I think that kind of homicide offence is repugnant to the Canadian people and I would strongly urge members to give serious consideration to that.
My final point is that I want to make abundantly clear what the minister is asking this House to approve and I have reason to believe that this House is going to approve it. It is a long way from being perfect. There are some amendments that are going to be considered. I have some amendments myself that I would like considered but here is what the bill does.
We have one extradition hearing. Charter issues will be dealt with in that Superior Court appeal. That means that the minister has a deadline to submit her signature
November 7, 1991

intent to extradition which would be reviewed at that one appeal. That is it.
This House of Commons, we as members of Parliament, has taken the seven-year option away and have put in a six-month option on the extradition. It could be three months. So you have an extradition hearing including charter issues. You have an appeal of committal of extradition, judicial review and surrender order of the Minister of Justice heard at the same time. That is it.
If the person being extradited after that short period of time wishes an appeal, he can have leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada; not guaranteed but leave to appeal. That ends it.
It would be a great accomplishment for the justice committee, for members of this House, if we could move with all haste to get it into committee. Let us look at the amendments that the NDP, the Liberals or the Official Opposition and the government would like to consider. I hope we can get it out of the House today. I hope it will move on to committee and be back here for third reading when we come back from our holiday.

I have a comment and a question, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I feel as if I should join in the general frivolity of the discussion but it is a serious matter.
Bill C-31 is designed to bring changes as has been pointed out in our Extradition Act. Many of us on both sides of the House must reflect on our own effort or lack of effort on this issue over the years to correct the flaws in the present extradition law.
It is very long overdue. As I will conclude at the end of my speech it hardly deals with the problem in all of its many aspects. The government has waited far too long to move decisively on this issue. The cost of that inaction is high first of all in material terms. Millions of dollars of taxpayers' money have been spent on unnecessary lengthy, highly publicized extradition cases instead of on research and development, education or other desirable things.
More important, the cost is expressed in human suffering of the victims' families in the case of Mr. Ng for example, the loss of widespread public trust in our system of justice, and the principle that a just punishment cannot be measured or recovered.
Canadian extradition law has come under a firestorm of controversy during the past several years. People are asking seriously if Canada has become a haven for dangerous criminals fleeing persecution in their own countries.
A New York Times article reported last year that there have been almost 260,000 murders across the U.S. since 1976. If even a tiny percentage of alleged American murderers began to flee to Canada, the cost and other consequences to Canadians would be enormous.
The lengthy appeals process in our extradition system of course was the heart of the problem because a series of orchestrated appeals both burdened our legal system and harboured foreign fugitives for years.
Nowhere has this been more evident than in the case of accused mass murderer Charles Ng, recently returned to California. Ng and an alleged accomplice, Leonard Lane, are suspected of having been involved in 25 violent criminal acts and 12 brutal homicides in northern California during 1985.
When the police in California apprehended Lane after a robbery attempt, he committed suicide. Mr. Ng however eluded capture and made his way to Calgary. He was spotted shoplifting in Calgary, shot at a security guard and served a four and a half year sentence in a Saskatchewan penitentiary. U.S. authorities soon initiated extradition proceedings.
In the judicial part of the process our Alberta Court of Queen's Bench ruled, Madam Justice Marguerite Tressler, that Ng could be found guilty on 19 of the 25 counts of violent crimes and the 12 homicides and was to be delivered to jail awaiting extradition to the U.S. authorities. His lawyer appealed to the Alberta Court of Appeal and approximately four years after Ng was arrested the three judges upheld the lower court decision. Quite recently, as members know, the Supreme Court of Canada refused to hear Ng's appeal of that appellate decision in Alberta.
All of Ng's appeals have been based on article VI of the 1976 extradition treaty between Canada and the U.S. which states: "When the offence for which extradition is requested is punishable by death under the laws of the requesting state and the laws of the requesting state do not permit such punishment for that offence, extradition may be refused unless the requesting state provides such assurances as the requesting state"-only lawyers could have drafted this-"considers sufficient that the death penalty shall not be imposed or, if imposed, shall not be executed". I am being candid.
The key is the term "may be refused" because the Minister of Justice decides which way to exercise the discretion. In 1989 Rudy Blanusa, accused of murdering two people in California, was extradited by former Justice Minister Lewis who opted not to seek the assurance that Blanusa would not face death.
By the way I might interest my friend from the New Democratic Party in the following case. In the 1970s a woman in Alberta was accused of being involved in a murder. Her co-accused was convicted. She left Alberta and went to California. She was finally picked up in Los Angeles. Do you know how long it took? As I understand it they picked up the accused, put her on the plane in Los


November 7, 1991

Angeles, flew her to Vancouver, and the RCMP picked her up when she got off the plane. I think the whole process took about three days. It has taken six years for us to uninvite Mr. Ng from our country.
There were also indications, as the member for Peterborough pointed out, that Charles Ng researched extradition laws in foreign countries including Canada. He came to Canada, specifically it would appear, because he knew the length and complexity of the Canadian extradition system and that he would face the death penalty in California.
I salute the member who just spoke for his concern about this issue and his consistent concern about this issue over the years. I will even quote him: "Fugitives such as Charles Ng or Joseph Kindler have more judicial options and opportunities available to them than does a Canadian citizen who is accused of committing a crime here in Canada".
Another glaring inconsistency in our system is an experience recounted to me of a judge who was appointed to a superior court in one of our provinces in Canada. That judge was denied a computer word processor to have in his office. Charles Ng had a computer word processor in his cell in Prince Albert paid for, one would assume, by the Canadian taxpayer. In other words, Canadian judges, at least in one province, cannot get word processor computers but people accused of 25 violent crimes in California can, at the taxpayers' expense.
In 1989, had it been the law, the proposed reform by the member for Peterborough and other MPs and I would not have prevented people accused of crimes from fleeing to Canada, but at least it would have reduced the number of manoeuvres of which they could avail themselves.
Under the proposed bill before us, the extradition hearing would still be presided over by a superior court judge or county court judge who would decide whether the fugitive should be committed to prison in view of the extradition. The next step would be the ability to appeal a decision to the appeal court of the province.
Those would be the only hearings available. It would eliminate the application for a writ of habeas corpus to the superior court and the ability to appeal the decision
Government Orders
of the appellate division to the Supreme Court of Canada.
After two court appearances the case would go automatically to the Minister of Justice. This would cut down significantly on the time frame for extradition but still protect the rights of the accused person.
Section 24 of the Extradition Act would also be examined. It states: "A fugitive who has been accused of an offence with Canadian jurisdiction, not being the offence for which the fugitive surrendered or who undergoing sentence upon conviction in Canada, shall not be surrendered until after having been discharged either by acquittal, by expiration of sentence, or otherwise." That would mean that the Minister of Justice would have the discretion to surrender incarcerated felons or allow them to serve their time. A decision would be made on a case by case basis.
Members of the Victims of Violence Society of Edmonton, now based in Ottawa, have estimated that it cost taxpayers over $1.5 million to keep Charles Ng in comfort in Canada. It was also stated by the member for Peterborough earlier that his office had received over
70,000	letters and 100,000 signatures on petitions from Canadians asking for the speedy extradition of Mr. Ng.
My own office has received more than 6,000 petition signatures. In short, the public outcry is enormous. In conclusion, the system in place must be streamlined so that Canada does not become or remain a haven for criminals from other countries and that criminals from other countries do not continuously burden our system and drain local economies.
A more streamlined system, founded on the same basic human rights principle but appended by the ideal of swifter justice, is required. Justice delayed is justice denied in these cases as in most cases. The changes proposed in Bill C-31 will probably come too late to help at least some of the families in the cases of Charles Ng, who was until recently able to delay his inevitable fate.
The case should bolster our resolve to make sure that no other criminal victimizes our country as well.
