Mr. Speaker, once again I am presenting my bill, Bill C-269, to Parliament. At this time I am aware that progress has been made on this issue. On the last occasion that this bill was considered it was referred to the standing committee on communications and was never subsequently considered by that committee which to me was a very disappointing matter on an issue which is so important to so many people across Canada.
The issue of copyright is one that has a very significant history and has been the subject of a tremendous amount of debate.
In 1985 after the consideration of phase I of the copyright legislation the minister of communications and culture, the Hon. Flora MacDonald, promised that there would be a phase II to the copyright legislation. Subsequently, we have had consultative committees that have been established with users and creators on those committees that made recommendations for certain exemptions for education, libraries and the disabled. These reports have sat on the shelf awaiting implementation by the government.
November 7, 1991

That committee report back in 1985 made those recommendations. We have had another committee report. There has been a tremendous amount of lobbying on this issue in the community. I myself have been involved in it since at least 1985 as a teacher in the city of North York and a media studies teacher and a member of the Association for Media Literacy. The copyright legislation was extremely important to us because basically being a media studies teacher is impossible with the existing legislation if one wishes to obey the law. Media studies teachers along with many other educators throughout Canada and many other users have virtually been breaking the law since this particular bill was introduced. Many of us were breaking the law before, but at least it was a little more liberal.
Phase I very clearly has given the authority over copyright to the owners of copyright exclusively.
There is no balance to the legislation. It does not recognize the legitimate rights of users. It does not reflect our society. It does not reflect the electronic age we now have and the types of communications necessary in this society. Many of us in Parliament continue to break this law. In the householders that we pass out there are often pictures and newspaper articles and we did not get the authority from the owners of these copyrights. If we did I am sure we would be spending an awful lot of time on rather useless correspondence.
Right now this particular bill has a long list of supporters. There are quite a number of individuals who support it but at present the Association of Universities and Colleges in Canada supports it as well as the Canadian Association of Research Libraries, the Canadian School Trustees Association, the Association for the Study of Canadian Radio and TV, Carleton University Instructional Media Services, Canadian Society of Copyright Consumers, the Alberta Whitecourt School District, the Protestant Regional School Board of Western Quebec, the Dundalk and Proton Community Schools in Ontario, the Canadian Centre for Studies in Publishing, the Metropolitan Toronto Separate School Board, the Eitz Chaim Schools in Toronto, the Ontario Secondary School Teacher's Federation District 13, North York, the Board of Education for the City of Etobicoke, North York Public Library Board, the Board of Jewish Educa-
Private Members' Business
tion, Seemars Engineering, CCH Canadian Limited, and the list goes on and on.
Clearly there are some contentious parts to the bill and some of these people would like to see certain amendments but they would like to see the bill considered and given implementation.
The Association of Universities and Colleges and the Canadian School Trustees Association were involved in forming this bill and I would like to describe it a bit.
It excludes any work that is the repertoire of a collective. It does not apply to works which are the property of a collective and which are available for a contract. It refers to all those works that are not currently available easily for people in educational institutions. It would allow the fair use for a limited number of purposes such as teaching, review, legislative or judicial proceedings, research, criticism, comment or media summary.
These are non-profit uses that are frequent in society. If one just thinks of the courts for a moment, frequently they have to look at documents. Under the existing legislation which has no exemptions and no limitations, other than the single one of the fair dealing which allows for individual, private study, there is no legal way in which any kind of legal work can be presented.
We have seen members stand up in the House with documents. If you are publicly displaying it, it is an illegal act at present. Therefore, it is simply impossible to obey the existing legislation.
This act is modelled basically on the American system. In the American system the factors which are considered and which are in this bill as well for determining whether a copyrighted work is being fairly used include the purpose and character of the use, including whether the use is for non-profit purposes, the nature of the work, in a case in which only part of the work is reproduced, the amount and substantiality of the part used in relation to the whole work and the effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the work.
It does allow a legal defence when you use a copyrighted work. It allows you to use it reasonably. It also allows organizations that own copyright to enter into negotiations in order to determine what is a fair use. It operates quite reasonably in the United States. Many Canadian teachers have resorted to contacting American

November 7, 1991
Private Members' Business
publishers and owners of copyright in order to access American materials, since it almost impossible to do it up here.
We have had a number of examples of teachers who belong to the Association of Media Literacy being able to contact magazines and television stations to get the right to use their material fairly. In Canada they cannot get that right. They might be able to get the right for a particular show, but they have to go through a long chain of people in order to get that particular right.
I tried that once and it took me eight different telephone contacts. All the way along the line people said: "Go ahead and do it. We don't care". However, because I was doing it for a particular project that was going to be circulated among teachers, I wanted to find out and I proceeded to do it. I finally got to the very end of the line and got permission. I was told how to do it and to send a letter. Unfortunately what happened was that the program I wanted to use was bumped from the television schedule and technically I could not have done it.
It is just ridiculous, the current procedure that one would have to go through in order to use material legally.
I asked some of the organizations involved with this issue what comments they would like to make on it at this point in time. The Association of Universities and Colleges says it wants phase II as soon as possible. It believes that my bill is a good interim piece of legislation while waiting for the government to introduce something, but it is concerned that even if phase II were announced there would not be enough time before an election for it to become law. I think that would be incredibly embarrassing to this government with a great number of people, given the commitments that have been made by the government in the past. Basically the association says that it thinks this bill would ensure at least a defence for people and fair access.
The director of Instructional Media Studies at Carle-ton University says: "It is important for Canadians to be able to study and to evaluate the media. There is a need to research the media and to display the findings. A department such as Mass Communications in Women's Studies needs to study specifics such as the portrayal of women in the media. Current copyright law restricts media study, making it difficult to teach the dissemination of it". Things such as taking a slide of a magazine article and putting it up on an overhead are illegal. It makes it very difficult to be referring to little pictures in a classroom.
The Canadian Association of Research Libraries says that it needs further amendments to the Copyright Act to ensure that Canadian students, researchers and scholars are not at a disadvantage when compared to their peers internationally. The inter-library loan network cannot work efficiently without certain exemptions as many publications are no longer available.
The Association for the Study of Canadian Radio and Television says that research is impossible under the current law. Copies of the whole work cannot be made for private study. Educators and researchers are forced to use American material because it is readily available for free, especially at the university level.
For example, the CBC has only four people working its sales department for education and does not have the time to work on copyright clearance, nor do the professors or researchers who need to use the material. The CBC has nothing available with clearance which is appropriate for university use, again sending users to the U.S. for material. They are not unwilling to pay reasonable royalties. In the U.S. Canadian works are available at less than half the cost they are in Canada. The current law is there to be broken, not complied with, as it is impossible to work under.
The Vancouver Community College Library Services' director says that in order for inter-library loan services to operate efficiently exemptions are necessary. Libraries already pay a higher subscription rate for journals which one would expect to cover use by more than one person. Inter-library services should be able to provide a copy of a work no longer available or rare to another library. They should be able to use material taped from the television for a limited time, 45 days, as is allowed in the U.S. They think that the classroom should not be considered a public performance arena. Educators should be allowed to do their jobs with fair access to Canadian material.
Right now costs are too high. They have found that most journals are willing to grant permission to copy for educational use when asked and without royalties, but this is a very time consuming process. By limiting access to information the Copyright Act only serves to put

Canadians at a disadvantage in the areas of research and education.
I am not against collectives. In fact my bill is designed to work with collectives. However, I am really disturbed about CANCOPY, the collective that is currently operating in Canada in the area of published print material. I think it has to operate in an ethical fashion and not by threats and intimidation. We have reports from UBC, Vancouver that in fact that is what it is getting.
The Association of Universities and Colleges has recommended to all its members that they not sign agreements with CANCOPY until it has decided what is an appropriate agreement, and it is getting threats from CANCOPY that it will be sued.
I think there should be guidelines to follow when establishing a collective. For example, I think its membership should be public. We have been trying to find out who are the members of CANCOPY and all we can get is a list of who are not the members. We know that a lot of people are not members. For example, the Canadian government is not a member. CANCOPY is going around claiming to have the copyright for all published material in Canada with these exceptions, as well as internationally with these exceptions that are listed here. In Canada the exceptions are: the Canadian Law Book, Nelson Canada, the Thompson group, Clarence Boon and Gladys Downes.
There are an awful lot of other people in Canada who publish material. Certainly if we start thinking about government publications, Canadian scientific journals, newspapers and magazines other than the Thompson chain, all children's authors and all textbooks, clearly it is outrageous to think that these authors have all been approached and all know that CANCOPY is purporting to sell their copyright to various bodies.
The Ontario government has in fact an agreement now with CANCOPY at a cost of $2 million which applies to boards of education in Ontario. It does not apply to the colleges and the universities, to the libraries or to the many other public agencies. It only applies to the boards of education.

In looking at the agreement I think it is extremely limited. First of all, as I said before this is just published print material. It allows one to copy a poem. It allows one to copy up to 10 per cent of the work and it allows, for example, one to copy a short story out of a textbook. I have found that a lot of what I was doing as a media studies teacher was certainly not that. There were lots of excellent Canadian textbooks with poetry and so on in the English curriculum, but in many other ways the kind of stuff one wants to copy is often in The Globe and Mail and on television. There are many other sources of material.
Another question is: What is CANCOPY going to do with the $2 million, because there is no proved mechanism now to distribute that money? We do not know who is going to get the money and we do not know who the membership is. There are an awful lot of people out there who I think would be rather surprised to think that their copyright has been given to CANCOPY.
Indeed we have a situation here which is chaotic and which is hurting various activities in the education field and the library field across Canada in a very visible way. I think all we have to do is go into a library and look at the line-ups at the copying machines of students who have to make one copy from one book they are supposed to be studying that is in the library.
When I went to an American university, Harvard, it would pass us out the copies. We had access to the material we needed to study. Now we have students standing in long line-ups. That is just one small example.
Teachers are intimidated. They are not using materials. They are using found materials that they themselves have developed, student materials and American material. I think there is a real ongoing inhibition on learning.
I have met with the new minister. I am pleased that he seems to be taking a greater interest in this topic and will shortly be bringing it to cabinet. He has promised to have legislation by the spring. I am hopeful that that legislation will accommodate many of my concerns and those of people in general, but I am very concerned about the timeframe.

Mr. Speaker, first and foremost I would like to congratulate the member for Don Valley North. She has done us a great service. It is a very good step forward.
There are certain parts of the bill that I think need to be examined a little more closely. The member can be very sure that she will see the support of myself and my party to move this forward in the committee so that we can examine some of the issues that she has brought to light and some of the ongoing issues which are the end result of a minister of that day. The then minister from Kingston and the Islands, in such a rush to put a crown on her head and be the first to have amended copyright law, did not really care about or pay much attention to the serious flaws in the first section of copyright. She subsequently has not fulfilled her promise nor have the subsequent ministers fulfilled their promise to bring in the second phase of copyright.
It was a bill that needed to be amended. It was a 1924 bill. It needed to be updated. This government did an update in 1988 with Bill C-60. If I could just say to my hon. colleague, it probably was one of the big nightmares of my life. I could also tell my colleague that there was a lack of interest by all members from the government side of the House. They did not attend the close to four months' worth of hearings and advised me that there was nothing in that bill to worry about. They said that there was no need for consultation and that all the answers were in that bill. When we finally started to unfold and look at this tangled web, to use another expression, we discovered so many flaws, so many errors that I cannot remember the number of amendments that were brought forward to the first phase.
The second phase which is the whole key to copyright, fairness and balance, never came to see the light of day. There is a fundamental belief by all fair Canadians who recognize that intellectual matter belongs to the creator. Whether it is a person in the artistic field, a writer, a
composer, a choreographer, a dancer or someone drawing the plans for a building, an architectural design, they have the right to the creative endeavour and to be paid for it.
Educators have never argued that right. What educators have said from their perspective is that they have a very serious responsibility, that is the future of our young people, the future of our country and the future as they train and educate.
I was fascinated to learn about the member's responsibilities as media teacher. Of course there has been tremendous technological change. There has been tremendous movement forward with respect to how one learns and the medium through which one learns today. If we recognize the hundreds and hundreds of hours in which children sit in front of a television set and how they absorb and learn as compared with how many hours they spend in school, that alone, in and of and by itself makes for the recognition that they need to have access on a spontaneous use basis to many of the creative and researched articles that are done on News Magazine, on The Journal and on certain of our Canadian documentaries. I well understand the frustration of all educators out there that are in contradiction of the law and that essentially teach law and order. They teach moral precepts in terms of comportment, behaviour, honesty and integrity. Yet the teaching profession is forced to misuse and go against the grain.
On the other hand as well, while this bill was providing for stopping the haemorrhage, the piracy of intellectual property, it did not look at the other side of the coin. It did not examine the need for use and the mechanisms of fair use.
One of my concerns about her bill is the term fair use. That is an Americanization of the approach that we want to have here in Canada. There is a fair balance that we have to find. I would hope that she would be open to examining that and the kind of change that would have to be made to her bill, which is fundamentally sound with a few little changes here and there.
If we talk about the copyright being an issue of balance-if you use it you pay for it, except in certain conditions and under certain constraints-I think that the creators would be happy as would the educators and the researchers.

One of the most moving briefs came from the Canadian Institute of the Blind about the young women and men who need to have enlarged print, who need to have it now, who need to be able to use it so that they can keep up with their other colleagues. There is nothing wrong with these young people. They have all the intellectual attributes of anyone else. The deficiency, if you may call it that, or the handicap is that of being partially sighted.
There are many ways in which one can help the partially sighted. Among them is projection of a daily newspaper text on to a screen and the production of an enlarged script for them that they are able to read. No, that is against the law. That is totally unacceptable.
I would think that the hon. member's bill should move quickly into committee so that we can look at many of these areas.
I do not know if the member is aware of one of the facts that really annoyed me. The Minister of Communications received a letter early in July and he has received a subsequent follow-up letter sent September 2 which included all the groups that the hon. member alluded to: libraries, school boards, universities, CEGEPs, CNIB. They wrote the minister and asked for a meeting.
The hon. member brought to our attention, and rightly so, that the consultant committees were set up. It was a great coup when the creators sat down with the users and with the Department of Communications and drafted a list of those things which could be considered exemptions, those things which could be considered available for spontaneous use because they are timely, they are today. The accident did not happen yesterday. The Berlin wall did not fall then. It fell now. They also wanted to advise him that because the second phase is so long in forthcoming what they negotiated is now no

longer totally useful because of changing technology. They wanted to share with the minister what new changes need to be made to the list which he presently had or his staff had on hand. Still there is no answer from the minister.
That is totally unacceptable. I am not blaming the minister. I am blaming the bureaucracy. The bureaucracy should know that. She is a very hard working parliamentary secretary and I know she will diligently bring this to his attention.
It would be very interesting to find out in this committee what CANCOPY is doing. We are in the midst of status of the artist legislation in which we are supposedly responding to the needs of individual artists, which we are not; where we are supposedly responding to a variety of concerns.
We should be calling these groups before us. Let us hear what the writers, the film makers, and the TV people have to say. Let us get down to the bottom of CANCOPY, in or out, fair or unfair. Let us know what can be done for the universities and the libraries and our students in particular especially with illiteracy, the school drop-out rate and the need for a good manpower training program. Why is it not being done?
Thank you very much for presenting the bill. We support it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member on an initiative that is really long overdue.
I have some concerns about the bill. However, certainly in terms of its over-all intent, we are very much in support of it. It is an initiative that has been needed for some time. The government has recognized the need to bring this in and we support it in its efforts. We would certainly like to see this bill move quickly to committee where I feel it could be strengthened somewhat and made into legislation that would provide effective support for those particular communities, such as the education community and the research community, that right now are often unknowingly in violation of copyright laws.

November 7, 1991
Private Members' Business
I come from a research and academic background. I was also an educator. I can remember when I was doing my graduate work some time ago. Graduate research involves copying large volumes of material for your own use in order to produce the thesis you may be working on. It is the nature of that kind of academic research that it has to involve that kind of activity.
Graduate students for years have been knowingly or unknowingly breaking copyright legislation. Universities have been. I would submit that every member's office in this House of Parliament in fact breaks copyright legislation in its day-to-day activities.
It is one of those areas in the whole field of communications where the the pace of technological change has outstripped our policy framework to manage that change.
A simple example would be as follows. A news article, a story, or a piece of literary work could easily be photocopied in an office in British Columbia. That photocopy can then be fed into a fax machine and transported electronically through satellite linkage and fibre optic linkage to an office here in Ottawa. That office can pick up the message either through another fax machine or through a fax modem built into a computer and print out that message. That is basically in violation of a copyright even though they are using legitimate means to communicate a message.
We have a really difficult situation here that requires changes to be made. The over-all intentions of the bill are good. In particular, reflecting back to the educational field, I think our educators need the widest range of choices available to communicate effectively with and teach our students of today.
Bill C-60, which was phase I of copyright reform, was passed back in June 1988. At that time the Minister of Communications indicated that educational exemptions and phase II of the copyright reform would not be long in coming. There was assurance given to this House at that time that the second round of amendments would in fact be introduced in the fall of that year. That was three years ago now. Successive ministers of communications have insisted that this phase II reform is just around the
comer. However that comer has been a long time coming.
Not only has this necessary reform been delayed too long, but certainly the policy direction of this government has remained very unclear. A year ago October the then Minister of Communications indicated in an unofficial speech that there was a change in policy. Instead of including exemptions proposed by two committees on phase II legislation, a new system was proposed by the then minister. Under that system all uses, including educational uses of copyrighted materials, would be subject to payment. Needless to say the outcry from the educational community was extreme and legitimate. It had been promised one thing and were now essentially being told another.
There have been mixed signals from the government in regard to phase II of copyright reform. That has caused the issue to become very confused, very agitated and very complex for educators, creators and people involved in non-profit academic research.
I would just like to give a couple examples of what people are up against without even really knowing it. It startles me as a former educator who taught in the sciences. I guess I broke copyright rules every day. I hope with that admission that the copyright cops do not come looking for me because I think it is indeed very common.
A poem written out in full on the blackboard for discussion in a class is a violation of copyright. A news program taped by a teacher, perhaps for an elementary class for discussion, is a violation of copyright. A rented film shown to a class is again a violation. Most educators are probably unaware of the fact that almost on a daily basis they are almost forced to break this law through their professional conduct.
Obviously the law is not working very well. It needs to be changed. This amending legislation does to some degree recognize the difficulty in making those changes.
Over the past little while my office has received a number of letters from educators right across Canada that are really concerned. They simply cannot contact every copyright holder. If there is an article they want to use for their class next day how are they going to write to the copyright holder and ask to use the material. It is simply impossible to function that way.
November 7, 1991

Educators have a right to know whether their actions contravene the copyright act. I think students, particularly those in post-secondary education, also have a right to know. They also have a right to be provided with the widest access to the information they need to pursue their education.
There are problems with the bill. I recognize that but I fully support its merits. In recognition of that we want to move this bill into committee stage so that we can listen to expert testimony from witnesses before the committee and then make the kinds of necessary amendments needed to make this legislation really work.
In the final analysis we have to ensure that there are built-in safeguards, provisions, and protections to ensure that educators and those involved in non-profit or educational academic research are given the freedom that is necessary to allow them to pursue their professional goals.
We concur in principle with the bill. Let us send it to committee and let us get good legislation out of this.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Nicole Roy-Arcelin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with a very outdated law: the current Canadian copyright law was proclaimed in 1924, and until two years ago was never substantially revised. This is a 68-year-old law that used such terms as "perforated rolls" and "mechanical contrivances". In the intervening years, we have seen the introduction of radio, television, photocopiers, audio and videotape recorders, computers, satellites and a variety of information storage and retrieval devices.
On the one hand, new technologies have greatly encouraged the creation and dissemination of Canadian creative works; they have helped in the actual production of such works and generated new methods and new markets for the exploitation of copyrighted works, thereby increasing the potential for financial compensation for rights holders.
On the other hand, while these technologies have helped disseminate the works of Canadian creators, they have allowed the use of such works without permission. Consequently, a host of complex legal problems have arisen, many of which require legislative solutions. We
Private Members' Business
began addressing these problems in 1988 when the 1924 Copyright Act was partially amended by Bill C-60 and the Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act.
The 1988 amendments made nine specific changes to the Copyright Act.
We increased criminal fines from a mere maximum of $200 to $1 million.
We gave explicit protection to computer programs; and enhanced moral rights to protect the reputation of the creator.
We enshrined a right of public presentation for artistic works; clarified the interface between copyright and industrial design.
We gave protection to choreography whether or not it has a story line; and we abolished compulsory licenses for the making of sound recordings, allowing for negotiated royalty fees within the marketplace.
Bill C-60 also encouraged the formation of collectives that represent the interests of copyright holders. Based on a concept which has worked well in the music industry for over 50 years, these collectives can be formed in all areas of copyright to negotiate licenses with the users of copyright materials.
Collectives provide users with quick and easy access to copyright materials. If the collectives and users are unable to agree on a fair royalty rate, either party may ask the Copyright Board to set the rate. As such, the amendments to the Copyright Act also broadened the mandate of the Copyright Board.
The changes I just mentioned were the beginning of the amendment process to an antiquated law. These amendments demonstrate a strong commitment by the government to proceed with further copyright revision to deal with other important issues. The amendments have also been welcomed and applauded by both the creator and user communities.
Bill C-269, before us today, deals with a copyright issue which requires careful attention. The government shares the hon. member's concerns and appreciates her efforts in attempting to find a solution to the complex area of the use of copyright materials for educational purposes. The issue here, however, is not whether to address the subject of exceptions but rather to determine the most appropriate method.

November 7, 1991
Private Members' Business
Bill C-269 presents one method of handling exceptions to the copyright law. The bill deals with "fair use", which would provide certain exceptions in the Copyright Act so that dealing with the copyright owner becomes unnecessary if a use is considered "fair" according to criteria set out in the law.
Viewed as a whole, Bill C-269 attempts to provide access to various users of copyright materials where such access is not available on a blanket license basis; that is, where a license is not available through a collective. However, ther are a number of problems inherent in the bill as well as external factors which require careful analysis and consideration.
Bill C-269 provides exceptions for schools and libraries, as well as other users. The bill is a significant departure from the concept of fair dealing contained in the current Canadian Copyright Act. Bill C-269's proposal is substantial. In some respects, it appears to be broader than the position reached during the dialogue which began several years ago between the government and creators and users, such as librarians and teachers. The government is using these discussions not simply as a reference point, but as an integral part of the current revisions governing exceptions that we will be proposing in the very near future. These discussions are crucial and must be taken into account in a comprehensive way in any amendments to the Copyright Act.
Copyright revision has always been a complex, controversial matter. One of the reasons for this is the balance that must be achieved between creators and users. But the provisions for exceptions are especially delicate; they are one of the clearest representations of that crucial need for balance. Given this need, the government made special efforts early on to ensure that both creators and users participated in the policy-making process for exceptions for libraries and educators.
In 1987-1988, two consultative committees were formed by the Department of Communications to discuss educational and library exceptions in the Copyright Act. In the beginning, creators and users came to the negotiating table at polar ends. Users wanted broad exceptions to allow them free access to works required for teaching and research and for library patrons. Creators were strongly opposed to such broad exceptions, since they perceived them as undermining the principle
of copyright and too greatly reducing royalties. After much debate over several years, which I understand was very lively at times, the two sides finally found some common ground.
The consultative committees agreed that specific exceptions for libraries and schools be set out in the law, as opposed to an exception of the idea of fair dealing. That way, schools and libraries would not be faced with the ambiguity of determining whether a certain activity would be considered fair dealing by the courts. Instead the exceptions would clearly outline the exact types of activities which would be freely permitted within the scope of the copyright law.
As I indicated earlier, the discussions which took place within these consultative committees will be used as the basis for the drafting of the educational and library exceptions in the next phase of amendments to the copyright act. The provisions we will be proposing are anticipated by creators and by the education and library communities. In addition, the council of ministers of education of Canada support these provisions.
I applaud and share my colleague's concern regarding the urgency and the importance of providing exceptions for educators and other users. The government's new amendments to the Copyright Act will be introduced in very short measure. I am confident that my colleague will find this to be a comprehensive package which strikes the appropriate balance between the rights of creators to fair compensation and the rights of users to have adequate access to copyrighted materials.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to applaud my colleague's initiative, a very interesting initiative indeed, and to thank my other colleagues for their very constructive comments. It was the hon. member for Don Valley North, if I am not mistaken.

If my memory serves me correctly, I believe this same member has a private member's motion and a petition on another important topic, family reunification. I think she should be commended for that. People already in this country are often separated for years from their spouses, children and other close relatives. I am delighted that she has taken this particular initiative as well. It is a serious problem that needs attention.
November 7, 1991

Let me address this one specifically. This member is providing leadership for her government and it is sadly needed not only in this area but in a number of others. I rose in the House of Commons today on a question and indicated that the government had in fact undertaken a number of initiatives which unfortunately had not gone very well in the area of education. I pointed out for example, the transfer of funds to colleges and universities; funds for training and retraining, research and development. I added as I recall, student aid.
I could have added copyright and I say that in this sense. When I talk to educational organizations across this country, the Canadian Federation of Students, the Association of Universities and Community Colleges of Canada, the Canadian Association of School Trustees and ask what their three major problems are I venture that copyright would be mentioned every single time.
This is a serious problem. It is a priority and I am delighted it is being dealt with. I hope that we can in fact proceed.
The question we have to ask is: Why has there been no action to date? What is the problem? It is a serious problem. People have identified it as such. It has been around for a long time. All kinds of organizations, people who talk to politicians and others have asked that it be dealt with. What is wrong?
I hate to say this, but it falls somewhat in line with the government's behaviour on a number of other dossiers. They are unable to solve a number of problems and this is one that needs to be resolved. We must not wait month after month, year after year before dealing with this. It is not necessarily easy, but we have some fundamental principles that we know are operative.
There is the creator of the work that must be rewarded. I believe that everyone wants that to happen. There is the learner that needs to use the material, as well as the teacher and the researcher. We know that has to occur. We also know that there are at times minimal uses that are very important in terms of preparing materials for teaching or research projects or what have you.
Private Members' Business
Therefore we have these fundamental principles in place. We know there must be a fair reward for the creator and fair use for those who need limited amounts of that creation in order to make a point in colleges, universities, schools and elsewhere.
The foundation is there. Who is affected by all of this?
I said it was a priority. It is a priority not only because it has been around for a long time. People are frustrated. They want a decision and they are feeling very awkward in terms of what is actually happening in classrooms today. My colleagues have mentioned that.
The students in colleges, universities, high schools, elementary schools and in certain instances, the teachers and professors also need some guidelines on copyrights as do researchers and research libraries. Some people have special handicaps or certain disabilities, if you wish, in terms of learning. Because there are limited amounts of material and because they have special needs, we need to deal with it and be able to help them as well.

What should we do now while we are debating this bill? I think it does give us some basis, some direction, some guidance, if you will.
I think it is time to hear from all sides, from people who want to talk to us about this bill, to listen to them carefully, as we are presently doing, and to take their suggestions, comments and insights into account in order to proceed.
I must repeat-and I want to be very honest about this because I think that a number of people do not see the dilemma-that there is a major problem. I talked about the students, the teachers, the researchers, the library workers and other people who are frustrated and do not know what to do. It is up to us to take this opportunity to proceed. So let us not let this chance go by.

Having said that, I believe this is a meaningful contribution. We have the basis for discussion and should now proceed and invite people to address the question so that we can improve upon the various sections that do need improvement.
I do not want to prolong my address. I simply want to propose that this subject matter be referred to the appropriate standing committee.

November 7, 1991
Adjournment Debate

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I would just like to understand what the member is proposing here.
He has suggested that the subject matter of this particular piece of legislation be referred to a standing committee. My concern with that is that standing committees are masters of their own destiny. Are we obliging the standing committee to look into this particular piece of legislation or are we obliging them to look into the whole matter of the Copyright Act? If we are doing that, are we not infringing upon the work and effort and independence, if you like, of the standing committee? I would like that clarified.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 19 of this year I asked the Prime Minister about the state of the economy and what he was prepared to do in light of the fact that we were in an absolutely stalled position in terms of the economy.
The results of the recession were having a very serious impact on my riding, and Montreal in particular, and certainly across the country. In answer to the questions that I posed on the economy, the statistics and on what the potential future was for the families, the seniors and for youth in my riding and the hope that they would have a job and have something to look forward to in terms of improving the quality of their lives, the Deputy Prime Minister promptly, in a sense, criticized the Statistics Canada study which said that less than 1 per cent improvement in the family incomes was the experience of the decade of the 80s.
He went on to laud his government's economic policies which have been one of high dollar-the highest since 1976-high interest rates and the wrong tax at the wrong time with the GST which created the recession, the results of which were shown in the Statistics Canada study.
I then asked a second question of the Prime Minister suggesting that the exaggerations, the lack of understanding, the lack of clarity, the lack of content and the lack of forthrightness in the response of the Deputy Prime Minister were unbecoming of the country and the nation at this time when there were great anxieties concerning a destabilized economy and a destabilized, very cynical public.
The Prime Minister said: "Never mind about the
600,000	Quebecers who are out of work", and he went on to laud the drug bill and the implications for new drugs
November 7, 1991

research and "never mind the whole business about generics."
The facts are that in my riding alone we need 463 units a year. The government has only built 300 units of social housing and we have 4,000 low income households in Cote de Neiges that pay more than 30 per cent of their income in rent and we need these new housing units.
The other fact is that one person in four knows poverty. Six hundred thousand are without work. We are the unemployment capital of Canada. Thirty-two per cent of the residents live below the poverty line, seven communities have more than 40 per cent poor, 374 centres distribute food at food banks and 80 do not even have enough food to distribute, 29 per cent of people under age 18 and 32 per cent of those over 65 live in poverty, 15,000 people are without homes, 4,000 of them sleep on the streets in Montreal, and a large number are the youth without work, without hope, and without any education.
That is where our big problem lies.
I want to draw attention to the fact that in Montreal alone 25,000 households now depend on food banks every single month, an increase of 23 per cent since last year. It is the fastest growing industry in Montreal.
My question was: "Mr. Prime Minister, what are you going to do in the face of these facts?" The answer was: "Increase the ability of drug producers to produce more drugs".

speakeroldname: Mrs. Nicole Roy-Arcelin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Mount Royal maintains that this government's policies are to blame for the fact that family incomes did not increase during the eighties and that Canadians have been hard hit by unemployment. Let me set the record straight.
When my government came to power in 1984, the economy was just recovering from a world-wide recession, aggravated by the poor administration of the previous government. That is the situation we inherited, and we were successful in doing something about it. In fact, we completely turned the situation around. Our economic policies helped to stop the drop in average
Adjournment Debate
family income which occurred between 1980 and 1984 under the previous government. Our policies also brought about real growth in family income for the first time since 1980.
In fact, between 1984 and 1989, there has been real growth in family income at the rate of 2 per cent per annum, which compares very favourably with the growth Canada experienced during the seventies. Mr. Speaker, I would also like to point out to hon. members that according to the study by Statistics Canada, the gap between rich and poor widened during the first three years of the eighties. In 1984, however, there was a general upturn which continued until the end of the decade.
Mr. Speaker, this government believes that jobs are the best income security for Canadians. I may point out that economic policies implemented since 1984 have created 1.6 million new jobs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 21, I asked the Prime Minister to respond to a call for help from food banks in Montreal by promising to organize a round table conference on poverty. I was referring to a recent study by Moisson Montreal which revealed that more than 25,000 households in Montreal now depend on food banks every month, an increase of 23 per cent since last year.
When the study was released, Sid Stevens, director of Sun Youth, the biggest food bank in Montreal, said that food banks were no longer able to meet the demand.

When Sun Youth opened its food bank in 1981, it was supposed to be a temporary service to help the poor during the recession. Mr. Stevens now says that food banks have become a necessity, a way of life, and now give out more than 4,000 food baskets a month.
Reverend William McCarthy, executive director of Montreal's Old Brewery Mission, said: "I have never seen it this bad in 30 years". The same message was conveyed by the director of Montreal Harvest, John Pasquini: "The demand for food is outweighing the supply. Governments have to make the plight of the poor an urgent priority".

Adjournment Debate

I have also been in touch lately with Le garde-manger pour tous, another food bank in my riding which mostly serves southwest Montreal. Those in charge said they also lacked the resources to respond to increased demand.
Mr. Speaker, Le garde-manger pour tous, Sun Youth, Moisson Montreal and The Old Brewery Mission are all saying the same thing: they can no longer meet the demand. They are asking all three levels of government to set aside their jurisdictional quarrels and consider how this problem can be solved.
Unfortunately there has been no response so far, and it seems the Prime Minister has not had time to visit Sun Youth. In fact, Mr. Stevens invited the Prime Minister to visit Sun Youth over a year ago.

Ele wanted the Prime Minister to see for himself how Sun Youth operates. Mr. Stevens added in a letter to the Prime Minister: "During recessions, the requests put on us for aid escalate to the point where we are unable to meet the demand. This is a time when we Canadians, politicians, corporate leaders and those of us involved in providing these charitable services must come together to overcome the problem our lesser fortunate compatriots are faced with".
To this invitation, the Prime Minister's office replied: "It is impossible to include this event in the Prime Minister's heavy agenda".
In May 1991 Mr. Stevens again wrote to the Prime Minister inviting him to visit Sun Youth. In September in another letter, Mr. Stevens informed the Prime Minister during the postal strike Sun Youth had over 1,000 seniors in one day lining up at the food bank asking for support. It was a record number.
When I raised this question with the Prime Minister, he said that he found the suggestion interesting, that he would look at it and that he would report back to me.
Sun Youth is still waiting for an answer, and so are the
53,000	Montrealers who now use food banks every month. I urge the Prime Minister to accept Mr. Stevens
invitation, and to accept the invitation that has been extended by the Sun Youth organization.
I hope that he will visit Sun Youth before Christmas. [Translation]

speakeroldname: Mrs. Nicole Roy-Arcelin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very concerned that many poor hungry Canadians depend on food banks. The people in charge of those banks see the misery and even despair of individuals who have to rely on that type of emergency assistance. In addition, they always have to try to obtain enough gifts of food.
I congratulate them on their work and their dedication to the needy. We face a complex multidimensional problem for which there are no easy answers. In many ways, this phenomenon reflects some deep changes in society.
We must face these changes, but we must also recognize that there are no one-dimensional solutions. We must try to deal with social and demographic changes. Given the available financial resources, we must try to preserve our social programs as much as possible. In particular, we must help Canadians acquire new job skills so that they can adapt to the demands of an ever-changing market.
We must therefore work on finding solutions to economic and social problems while striving to ensure that all Canadians can live in dignity, with suitable food and adequate housing.
To solve the human and social problems confronting us, we must put the country's finances in order and that is why the government is determined to reduce the deficit. We cannot go on indefinitely allowing a national debt as big as ours-$15,000 for every man, woman and child-to continue to grow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question on June 17 was: Will the minister assure the women of Canada that there will be no further substantive cuts both to funding for women's programs and to funding for women's groups. Will he restore funding to pre-1988 levels and index such funding?

November 7, 1991



May I remind the minister that women make up more than half the population of Canada-52 per cent. In a democratic society, the needs and concerns of more than half the population must be taken into consideration.
Women are not a special interest group. We should enjoy complete access to funding, funding I might add that is not uncertain, funding that is not insecure or precarious and funding that does not teeter on the brink of the government's own idea of what the fiscal imperatives are.
While I commend the government for the step forward it is taking in the direction of understanding such things as violence against women-and by the step forward, I mean only the appointment of the Canadian panel on Violence Against Women-I find such a commitment whose price tag is $10 million and a commitment, as I say that I appreciate, at odds with its unwillingness to fund other programs for women. This is not something that can be dealt with on a single initiative. It is something that must be dealt with on numerous initiatives.
Just today we received Living Without Fear, the response of the government to the report of the subcommittee on the status of women entitled "The War Against Women". This is effectively what I am talking about. In this report there are many pretty words, but there is very little for the women of Canada to hang their hopes on. We read such words as support vis-a-vis such words as funding.
Believe me, Mr. Speaker, it is the word funding that we need to hear. It is the word funding that means everything to the women's groups that are hanging by a thread out there in every province and territory in this country.
These groups and the persons who work for them, most often on a volunteer basis or on wages that put them squarely in the category of the working poor, are a primary source of information for the members of the Canadian panel on violence against women. It seems to me unfair that they should suffer, that they should have to take low salaries and poor conditions because of their commitment to an ideal that the government talks about being committed to as well.
Adjournment Debate
That is why it is so crucial that these groups know that funding will not be cut off, not in next year's budget or the budget after that. It is also crucial that the funding be indexed. These women work in conditions, as I have already stated, that are not of the best. They need to know that their programming and their very futures which are so crucial to women in crisis in their communities will carry on. They need to know that the government's commitment or alleged commitment to true equality between the sexes extends to them, the soldiers in the front lines of the battle.
Consequently I urge the government to let the women of Canada know just what its real commitment is to this urgent issue. It is time to close the credibility gap and the hypocrisy and let us know just what exactly is going on with funding.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax is asking the government not to cut women's programs in the Secretary of State this year. Well, her wishes have been answered, there were no cuts in the budget for this year.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State, like all members in this House, is very sensitive to women's issues. We meet quite often with the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and I think I can say that, despite the fact that we do not always see eye to eye, we maintain an excellent working relationship with the committee, which we wish to continue.
The Secretary of State, along with the Minister responsible for the Status of Women, have demonstrated their commitment to stopping family violence. We have committed $6.6 million over four years to that end. We have targeted underprivileged women, women in remote areas and also native women who face the same kind of problems. We also created a new committee of men and women whose mandate is to look at family violence. I will conclude by saying to the hon. member, who has a keen interest in women's issues, that governments should not be the only ones to act, women themselves should get involved and should fund national committees whose role would be to help our sisters get out of their plight.

Mr. Speaker, nearly a month ago, I had a question for the Solicitor General, but in his absence it was answered by the Minister of Justice. The question referred to a constituent of mine who worked for the Canadian Security Intelligence Service-CSIS, our own secret service. I raised with the minister the problem of my constituent who was contaminated by bacteria or substances during a search of debris or residues of the fire at the Soviet consulate in January 1987.
Since he was a resident of Saint-Bruno, he came to my office and said: "Listen, I asked CSIS for compensation, and I asked them what the contaminant was. Was it a bacteria or some kind of product that the Soviet Union put on its papers or on objects that burned in the fire?" He never got an answer, and he was fired.
I know there is a case before the courts involving this agent of our secret service, but this does not prevent the government from being fair to a person who did an honest day's work for the government and simply wants to know what is wrong and whether he can get compensation, since he can't work as a result of the respiratory infection and problems he now has as a result of this search.
There are other questions, Mr. Speaker, but the main one is: Who authorized this search? Was it a spontaneous fire or did we set the fire?
Finally, I am not asking these questions because I am a great big paranoid Quebecer, but the fact is, we in Quebec are used to seeing our bams burnt and our membership cards stolen. So I would like some specific answers to these questions from the minister.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want my hon. colleague to know that the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada did bring to the attention of the Solicitor General the question he raised in this House on October 11.
My colleague acknowledged, when he first asked this question, that he knew the issue was before the courts. As everyone knows, when legal proceedings are ongoing, the Solicitor General cannot interfere or make any statements that might cause prejudice.
My colleague referred to the health status of his constituent. I just want to tell him the government and CSIS are well aware of their responsibilities and they know they have to ensure the health and security of all their employees, not just those ones, but all of their employees. They take their responsibilities very seriously and will continue to do so. When it was created, the service applied Treasury Board policies and guidelines on occupational health and safety. Since March 1986, CSIS had complied with the provisions of Part II of the Canada Labour Code which governs issues of occupational health and safety. It also has an official mandate and has concluded a memorandum of understanding on this matter with its unionized and non-unionized employees. Some funds have been earmarked for the safety requirements of buildings and projects.
As for my colleague's comments, which some media have also made regarding CSIS's activities, government policy is not to comment on any CSIS operations.
